articles.title_orig: Stock futures rise slightly as investors eye AI trade, brace for more data and earnings: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures rise slightly as investors eye AI trade, brace for more data and earnings: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Americans were unequivocal at the ballot box this week as they expressed disdain for tech billionaires and mistrust of artificial intelligence. With that backdrop, Anthropic is about to try to go public.
The AI company is gearing up for a potentially historic IPO, likely targeting mid-November for its Nasdaq debut. CNBC reported on Friday that Anthropic investors see the company aiming for a valuation of $1 trillion to $1.5 trillion, down from a target of $2 trillion that had been floated in recent months.
From Wall Street to Main Street, it's becoming a tougher environment for Anthropic. The Nasdaq on Thursday suffered its steepest drop in 19 months, and it's down to start November after October marked its worst month since March 2025. Chipmakers and neoclouds, the companies most closely tied to the AI buildout, are getting hit the hardest.
Voters rebuked AI in Tuesday's midterm elections, while sending Democrats to sweeping congressional victories across the country. Candidates who advocated for more stringent AI regulation won handily in states like Michigan, Ohio, Texas and Georgia, which will all now have Democratic governors, and local communities opposed data center-related ballot measures in 40 out of 41 cases .
More than half of voters said AI data centers were a "crucial" or "major factor" in who they supported for Congress, according to an exit poll from NBC News.
"People don't want a data center going near them if it's just going to house AI that's going to help a big tech company profit," Maura Austin, a behavioral scientist at the University of Virginia, told CNBC. "What Anthropic is doing when they're going public with such a high valuation is they're really leaning into that big tech, billionaire kind of caricature. I expect that's not going to go well with the public."
Anthropic has long tried to position itself as a safety-conscious company that takes AI's potential risks and benefits seriously. CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the company alongside a handful of researchers who defected from OpenAI , now its chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude , and it primarily sells its products and services to other businesses.
The company's enterprise focus has helped it avoid becoming the public face of AI, leaving that distinction to OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman . But with Anthropic poised to become the first pure-play AI company to hit the public market, minting a number of new billionaires and many more millionaires in the process, a heightened level of scrutiny is coming.
"Being a public company, just that by itself pushes you in the limelight," Reena Aggarwal, a professor of finance at Georgetown University, said in an interview. "And then AI is such a hot-button issue that Anthropic will be in the limelight even more."
Matt Kennedy, a senior IPO market strategist at Renaissance Capital, said that's not necessarily a bad thing for Anthropic.
Public markets force greater transparency, he said, and the company could attract new users through its debut. And since AI has become such a mainstream conversation topic, several private companies are already household names.
"I would say that a public company does not deserve more criticisms than a comparable private company," Kennedy said. "So Anthropic should not be put in a harsher public spotlight than OpenAI just because it's public."
Anthropic declined to comment.
AI backlash accelerated over the summer after a series of high-profile safety and security incidents rattled the public. As concerns mounted, the debate over data centers intensified, while tech's hyperscalers  simultaneously boosted their forecasts for capital expenditures, each reaching into the hundreds of billions of dollars.
Anthropic and OpenAI depend on state-of-the-art data centers to train models and serve customers, and they're trying to build out capacity as quickly as possible to meet demand. Anthropic said in an amended IPO prospectus this week that it has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion , "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure."
Americans grappling with inflation and stubbornly high gas prices have grown worried that the facilities could exacerbate environmental harms, raise utility bills and contribute to job loss. For many, a proposed data center in their backyard became the physical manifestation of the widespread antipathy toward AI.
In the risk factors section of its prospectus , Anthropic said opposition to data center development has become more organized across jurisdictions, and that the company's public profile could draw particular scrutiny to projects associated with it.
Nicole Greene, an analyst at Gartner, said she expects that Anthropic's executives have long been prepared to contend with AI backlash, especially given the disruptive nature of the technology.
"There's going to be big emotions," Greene told CNBC. "With big emotions and feelings — fear and excitement — comes heightened scrutiny."
Amodei acknowledged the souring sentiment around AI in a post on X in August. He said it's the result of a "crisis of trust," and that people believe companies, the government and the tech industry are always "cooking up some new way to screw them over."
Rebuilding public confidence is going to be an uphill battle as the company begins providing quarterly financial updates.
The University of Southern California published a survey on Monday that found that 71% of respondents don't trust big tech companies to act in society's best interest "at all" around data center development.
"Once you've lost trust, it's hard to gain it back," Wändi Bruine de Bruin, a professor at the University of Southern California's Schaeffer Institute, said in an interview. "The numbers are not good."

articles.title_orig: Iran acquires oil facilities in China to bypass US sanctions, leaked document shows
articles.title_zh: Iran acquires oil facilities in China to bypass US sanctions, leaked document shows
articles.content_orig:
Iran is using oil terminals and storage facilities in China to keep sanctioned tankers operating despite US restrictions, according to a confidential document obtained by Iran International and information from Oil Ministry sources.
The document is a confidential letter from Hamid Bovard, the former head of the National Iranian Oil Company and current acting oil minister, responding to a highly confidential letter Ali Shamkhani, a former secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, sent to then-supreme leader Ali Khamenei.
Shamkhani, who served as Khamenei's political adviser, had described oil sales under President Masoud Pezeshkian as disastrous. Both Shamkhani and Khamenei were killed in US-Israeli strikes on February 28, 2026.
In his letter, Bovard criticized the administration of former President Ebrahim Raisi for its policy of using newer vessels and described an arrangement developed under Pezeshkian with what he characterized as covert cooperation from China.
According to Bovard, Iranian authorities instructed trusted oil intermediaries to continue using sanctioned vessels capable of docking at designated ports.
Bovard said Iran's Foreign Ministry negotiated with China to acquire port facilities and oil terminals, establishing a hub for sanctioned Iranian crude.
Tehran also secured long-term leases on large oil storage facilities in several Chinese locations, allowing it to sell Iranian crude directly in the Chinese market.
Under the arrangement, vessels belonging to Hossein Shamkhani, Ali Shamkhani's son and the owner of a fleet of tankers commonly described as a shadow fleet, transport Iranian oil to docks in China controlled by Tehran. The facilities allow the vessels to continue delivering oil despite US sanctions.
The arrangement is designed to reduce the impact of US sanctions on Hossein Shamkhani's shipping operations. The US Treasury has sanctioned 51 vessels linked to him.
For years, Iran has worked with China to sell oil through trusted intermediaries to small independent Chinese refineries, known as "teapot" refineries. The United States has repeatedly sanctioned companies involved in these transactions, but the use of intermediaries helps shield China's major banks and three largest oil companies from US sanctions.
Iran's oil terminals and storage facilities in China
Two sources in Iran's Oil Ministry told Iran International that Tehran has acquired control of port facilities at three locations in China. One is in the Ningbo-Zhoushan free trade zone, where Iran gained control of a terminal by helping build several smaller transit facilities.
Tehran also secretly acquired stakes in smaller docks at the ports of Qingdao and Pant in China's Shandong province, according to the sources.
The docks are located near pipelines, allowing Iranian crude to reach Chinese refineries quickly without being transferred to other vessels.
Iran has also purchased seven oil storage tanks in China, allowing it to ship crude to the country before securing buyers.
Four large Iranian-owned oil storage tanks are located at the ports of Dalian and Huizhou and in the coastal cities of Dongying and Weifang.
The Oil Ministry controls three other large storage tanks in the Zhoushan area of the Ningbo-Zhoushan archipelago, according to Iran International's sources. They are the Kamergi tank on Aoshan Island, a tank at the Shulanghu Island terminals and another in the Zengyamuo oil zone.
Two months ago, Iran International published a document showing that Mohammad Javad Bavand, a special assistant to the oil minister, instructed oil intermediary Mohammad Hadi Momenin, who owed $2 billion, to use a vessel belonging to Hossein Shamkhani to deliver oil for storage at one of the Chinese ports.
China also earns revenue from storing Iranian oil. Nearly two years ago, Reuters reported that 25 million barrels of Iranian crude were stranded in storage facilities in China and that Tehran had paid $450 million in storage fees.
China distances itself from Iranian oil
Despite these arrangements, the confidential correspondence suggests that Tehran was facing growing pressure from its main oil buyer.
Bovard's confidential letter to Khamenei's office indicates that China had begun distancing itself from Iranian oil even before the 40-day war. According to the letter, Beijing rejected Tehran's request to increase crude oil import quotas for Chinese refineries, increased imports from Venezuela and demanded deeper discounts on Iranian oil.
Two months ago, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said at the launch of an initiative to economically isolate Iran that China and the United States had more in common than differences. He said China obtained 50 percent of its energy needs from the Persian Gulf and supported the free flow of maritime trade through the Strait of Hormuz.
Hossein Shamkhani's grip on Iranian oil trading in Dubai
Throughout the confidential letter, Bovard criticizes Ali Shamkhani, suggesting that his primary concern was protecting his son's interests in the oil trade rather than Iran's oil sales.
Bovard alleged that Hossein Shamkhani used Iranian government loans to purchase vessels but deployed them to transport Russian oil rather than Iranian crude.
According to Bovard, Hossein Shamkhani received Iranian oil on consignment without providing collateral and sold it on the market. Bovard portrayed the United Arab Emirates as Shamkhani's exclusive trading domain, saying the Oil Ministry had effectively become his agent rather than the other way around.
Former lawmaker Ahmad Amirabadi Farahani recently said the then-head of NICO, the National Iranian Oil Company's international trading arm, had barred Hossein Shamkhani and three other oil intermediaries from selling Iranian crude because they owed several billion dollars.
According to Bovard's confidential letter, Ali Shamkhani told Khamenei that Iranian oil had been sold at a discount of 50 cents per barrel under former President Ebrahim Raisi, compared with $9 per barrel under Pezeshkian. The Oil Ministry disputed Shamkhani's figures.
In September, Iran International reported that Mohammad Javad Bavand, a special assistant to the oil minister, had assigned four oil intermediaries, including Hossein Shamkhani, to sell 86 million barrels of Iranian crude at an 8.5 percent discount. The arrangement followed the transfer of oil sales from a network linked to the Intelligence Ministry to one linked to the intelligence arm of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Oil intermediaries discussed possible collapse of Islamic Republic
Former lawmaker Ahmad Amirabadi Farahani said during a debate that four oil intermediaries met at Charlie restaurant in Dubai hours after Ali Khamenei was killed in US-Israeli strikes. He said they declared that the Islamic Republic was collapsing and that they no longer needed to return proceeds from Iranian oil sales.
The Islamic Republic remained in power, but Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad was later dismissed following Shamkhani's letter to Khamenei.
Two weeks ago, Hossein Ghorbanzadeh, a board member of Persian Gulf Petrochemical Company and an associate of parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, told the Fars news agency that Paknejad's dismissal, carried out three weeks earlier, had originally been planned for Esfand, the Iranian calendar month spanning February and March.
Ghorbanzadeh said President Masoud Pezeshkian had told a cabinet meeting that Khamenei asked him to dismiss Paknejad over his handling of the crisis involving oil intermediaries. Khamenei's death and the outbreak of the 40-day war delayed the dismissal, he said.
Success will depend less on Washington’s ability to track shipments than on persuading governments, banks and suppliers to stop them.

articles.title_orig: DoorDash Shareholders Aren’t Convinced the Company Can Take On Amazon
articles.title_zh: DoorDash Shareholders Aren’t Convinced the Company Can Take On Amazon
articles.content_orig:
DoorDash employees might have to make fewer LinkedIn connections as a result of their employer's $17 billion deal to buy Instacart.
The food-delivery service told employees as much in an internal question-and-answer document filed with the SEC on Thursday.
"Can I connect with Instacart employees on LinkedIn?" reads one of the questions in the document.
"Not at this time," the answer says. "Please do not request any new connections with any Instacart employees on LinkedIn, even if you have a prior relationship."
The guidance shows that a pending takeover can change life inside the companies involved, sometimes for long periods. Merging companies must remain independent competitors, limiting employees' ability to coordinate or share sensitive information.
The document tells employees not to accept LinkedIn connection requests from Instacart employees, and that the two companies must continue to operate separately until the deal closes. DoorDash and Instacart said they expect the purchase to close either at the end of 2027 or in the first half of 2028.
Companies planning a merger or acquisition will often take steps to prevent employees from engaging in so-called gun-jumping, or behaving as if the deal is already done, something that could thwart the deal before it's completed. This might include sharing competitively sensitive information, coordinating on pricing or bidding, or discussing jobs with people at the other company without authorization.
"You're supposed to continue to act like independent competitors until the deal closes," said David Gelfand, senior counsel specializing in antitrust law at Cleary Gottlieb, and former deputy assistant attorney general for litigation in the antitrust division of the US Department of Justice.
By asking employees to refrain from certain LinkedIn connections, the companies could be trying to prevent brain drain, said Chris Selland, a lecturer at Northeastern University's D'Amore-McKim School of Business.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
DoorDash and Instacart already compete in the same industry. Discussions between employees could lead one company to hire employees from the other — bringing valuable connections, such as customer contacts, with them. "That could blow up the whole agreement," he said.
However, several M&A experts told Business Insider they'd never heard of employees at companies undergoing a deal being barred from connecting on LinkedIn or any other social media platform.
DoorDash declined to comment.
Whether Instacart and DoorDash are acting sensibly, or imposing an overly broad restriction on ordinary employee behavior is "a great antitrust examination question," said William Kovacic, a former FTC chairman and the director of George Washington University's Competition Law Center.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia investigates CEO Jensen Huang amid allegations he was target of Chinese intelligence effort
articles.title_zh: Nvidia investigates CEO Jensen Huang amid allegations he was target of Chinese intelligence effort
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia has launched an independent investigation of its co-founder and CEO, Jensen Huang, over allegations that he was the target of an intelligence effort by China.
The allegations center around a Chinese business executive named Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence agencies believe was an asset of China's Ministry of State Security, the country's main intelligence agency.
The CIA, NSA and ODNI did not immediately respond to CBS News requests for comment.
The New York Times reported last month that U.S. authorities were investigating Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, a former executive of the Singapore-based Megaspeed, which buys AI chips from Nvidia. The report claims Jensen Huang had a close relationship with Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials believe was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security.
Jensen Huang, in a message to Nvidia employees Sunday, admitted to being "unfaithful" to his wife and apologized for hurting her and their children, although he did not name the woman involved. "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," he said.
"The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort," Nvidia's board of directors said in a statement Sunday. "A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation."
The board said it had no reason to believe that the company's secrets or national security were compromised.
"The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders," the statement said.
China has rejected allegations of a Chinese espionage operation targeting Jensen Huang, describing the claims as "groundless speculation," CBS News partner BBC News reported.
A company spokesperson said Jensen Huang "fully supports the review" and is committed to continuing to lead the company.
Jensen Huang said he had fallen short of his responsibilities to the company's employees, board and shareholders. He said he is "fully committed to NVIDIA" and will work to earn back their trust.
"Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, NVIDIA's Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation," he said in a statement. "I support the investigation and will cooperate fully."
"I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American," he added.
Alice Huang was previously a television reporter in China before becoming a top executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, which has become one of Nvidia's biggest customers in Southeast Asia. Megaspeed bought more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the past two years, according to the Times.
Asked about the report on Sunday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he couldn't comment, saying it was an "internal corporate matter."
Nvidia, the world's most valuable company, has regularly surpassed Wall Street's earnings expectations in the past three years since its high-end chips emerged as AI's best building blocks. The Santa Clara, California-based company reported quarterly profits of $59.69 billion in August.
Olivia  Gazis and The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

The gradient electrodes – designed to overcome the current trade-offs of conventional uniformly soft or rigid electrodes – were integrated into a commercial electroencephalogram (EEG) cap and tested during rest over the span of 14 hours.

articles.title_orig: Society needs to act to help white working-class pupils, inquiry says
articles.title_zh: Society needs to act to help white working-class pupils, inquiry says
articles.content_orig:
Action from "across society" is needed to help improve the educational outcomes of white working-class children, the co-chair of an independent inquiry looking into the issue has said.
The inquiry's first report, published this summer , concluded that once-in-a-generation reforms were needed to fix a system "not serving the interests of white working-class children".
The next phase will focus on early years children and teenagers aged 14 to 19, aiming for a stronger start at primary school and improving older students' routes through education into successful careers.
Education Secretary Lucy Powell said she was "backing" the inquiry to "get to the heart of the barriers holding children back".
Inquiry co-chair and former education secretary Baroness Morris said the next phase of the inquiry's work will consider "what needs to be done".
"This isn't just the responsibility of schools but calls for action from across society," she said.
The Independent Inquiry into White Working Class Educational Outcomes was commissioned by the multi-academy trust Star Academies, and is supported by the Department for Education.
It spoke to thousands of young people and their parents, as well as hundreds of teachers.
Education data about white working class pupils was also analysed as part of the year-long review, looking at the 1.25 million young people in England who are white British and in receipt of free school meals.
The inquiry found a growing belief among white working-class families that the current education system does not guarantee future success.
In the summer, the inquiry also acknowledged that the true scale of white working-class disadvantage is "likely to be substantially larger", as the education data they looked at did not include families who were on low incomes but did not receive free school meals.
Since then, all families receiving Universal Credit have become eligible for free school meals .
Under the new phase of the inquiry, practical recommendations for government, schools, colleges and other organisations working with white working-class communities will be developed.
This action will include a research programme looking at the routes taken by teenagers aged 14 to 19, investigating how schools can work with communities to provide clearer pathways into further study and successful employment.
The new phase of the inquiry will also look at how schools can ensure the transition from primary to secondary school builds strong foundations.
"Right now, too many white working-class children are falling behind at every stage of their education," Powell said.
"That is why I am backing this independent inquiry to get to the heart of the barriers holding children back - from their first steps into school, through to the opportunities and choices they have as teenagers into further study, training or work."
It comes after Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced plans to open up new technical routes from age 14 in England over the summer.
The prime minister said he was "on a mission" to reduce the number of young people not in education, employment or training - known as "Neet".
Currently, nearly a million young people are classed as Neet.
Former minister Alan Milburn's interim report found that children who are not school-ready at aged four or five are nearly three times as likely to be Neet by ages 16 to 17.
A final report by Milburn is expected to set out his recommendations for tackling the issue in the coming weeks.

articles.title_orig: NASA opens recruitment for its next generation of astronauts
articles.title_zh: NASA opens recruitment for its next generation of astronauts
articles.content_orig:
The NASA logo is seen at NASA's Johnson Space Center, Friday, Aug. 28, 2026, in Houston. Karen Warren/AP hide caption
If you have dreams of going to the moon, you now have a chance. NASA is accepting applications for those interested in becoming an astronaut.
The candidates selected to be astronauts would not only test spacecraft but would also live and work on the moon in a future moon base, said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman in a statement released on Saturday.
"Those missions will demand technical excellence, sound judgment, teamwork, and courage," the statement said. "NASA's astronaut corps has always called on remarkable Americans willing to take on extraordinary challenges in service to the nation."
There are currently 32 active astronauts in NASA's astronaut corps. Since NASA missions began in the 1960s, the agency has selected 370 people to train as astronauts, according to the agency.
The applicant process is extremely competitive. Out of more than 8,000 applicants for NASA's last astronaut class, only 10 candidates were selected.
While any U.S. citizen can apply and there is no official age restriction, applicants will need to have a master's degree in a STEM-related field such as engineering or math.
In a recent change, a nursing degree qualifies.
"Nursing degrees are now included in the STEM definition," Anna Schneider, NASA spokesperson, told NPR on Sunday. "Master's-level nursing degrees now meet the minimum educational requirement, whereas nursing degrees were previously excluded."
In addition, NASA is requiring a minimum of three years of related professional experience after completing a degree.
In lieu of a master's degree and working experience, NASA will consider those in a PhD program (in STEM), doctors or pilots with extensive flight experience.
FILE - This detail of a July 20, 1969 photo made available by NASA shows astronaut Neil Armstrong reflected in the helmet visor of Buzz Aldrin on the surface of the moon. Neil Armstrong/NASA via AP hide caption
If chosen, the selected astronauts will undergo training that will last for two years. NASA said astronauts will prepare for critical and difficult missions such as landing near the moon's South Pole.
To achieve its goal of returning humans to the moon in 2028 – the first time since 1972 – NASA is relying on private companies such as Blue Origin and SpaceX to develop systems and spacecraft.
During a Nov. 7 press conference on the Artemis III moon mission's progress, Isaacman said he is "very confident" the mission will launch in 2027.
The starting salary is $164,395 and applications will be received through Dec. 3.
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Opens Independent Probe Into CEO Amid China Spy Allegations, Raising Security Concerns
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Opens Independent Probe Into CEO Amid China Spy Allegations, Raising Security Concerns
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang "is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA," the company said.
Tech giant NVIDIA has announced an investigation of its CEO amid allegations that he was the subject of an intelligence-gathering effort by the Chinese.
"The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort," the company said in a statement Sunday, adding that a "committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation."
Jensen "fully supports the review" and will cooperate with it, the NVIDIA statement further said.
"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," according to the statement.
"The Board prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders," the statement further said.
"The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team," according to the statement.
The New York Times reported late last month that Huang, who runs the world's largest computer chip manufacturer, was targeted by a Chinese espionage plot centered around a woman they identified as Alice Huang, a top executive at Singapore-based data company Megaspeed, whom U.S. intelligence officials determined was funneling information to Beijing and had developed a "close relationship" with Jensen Huang.
The Chinese government has denied the allegations, calling them "baseless and purely slanderous smears against China."
Neither Alice Huang nor her employer, Megaspeed International, responded to ABC News' request for comment after the New York Times story broke.
"Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected" and are part of Jensen Huang's job, an NVIDIA spokesperson told ABC News at the time.
However, NVIDIA on Sunday shared with ABC News an internal message Jensen Huang sent to employees, in which he said he was "unfaithful" to his wife.
"My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry," the message said, in part. It did not name Alice Huang nor any other person.
Addressing NVIDIA staff, partners and shareholders, Huang went on to say "my responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence."
"I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American," Huang's message said.
Following the New York Times report, congressional Republicans on the Select Committee on China sent a letter to Jensen Huang requesting that he appear for a closed-door briefing Nov. 18 concerning his relationship with Alice Huang.
"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's access to sensitive U.S. technology and information," the letter said, in part. It is not known if Huang will appear before the committee.
“Today’s news will not slow NVIDIA. Jensen is committed to continuing to lead NVIDIA as CEO without interruption," an NVIDIA spokesperson told ABC News Sunday.

articles.title_zh: Drone attack suspends production at Iraq’s Khor Mor gasfield
articles.content_orig:
A drone attack on the Khor Mor gasfield in the semi-autonomous Kurdish region of northern Iraq has caused a fire at the facility and cut power to the region, according to Iraqi and Kurdish officials.
The Sunday night attack left more than 70 percent of the Kurdish region without power.
It was not clear who was responsible for the attack or whether it was related to the United States and Israel’s war on Iran.
Al Jazeera’s fact-checking agency Sanad has verified footage of smoke and flames rising from the vicinity of the gasfield in the Sulaimaniyah governorate.
Omid Ahmed, spokesperson for the Kurdistan Regional Government’s Ministry of Electricity, said the attack suspended gas supply to power plants in the cities of Erbil, Sulaimaniyah, Bazian, Chamchamal and Duhok, the official Iraqi News Agency (INA) reported.
The strike knocked between 2,500 and 2,800 megawatts of electricity generation off the grid, he said.
He added that the ministry would provide electricity to critical facilities, such as hospitals and water treatment plants, by operating hydroelectric power stations and other plants that run on alternative fuel.
Al Jazeera’s Peter Smith, reporting from Baghdad, cited security sources as saying the explosive-laden drone struck the Khor Mor gas storage facility, reducing the energy grid’s capacity by 70 to 80 percent.
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said there were no casualties as a result of the attack, based on an initial assessment, the INA reported.
Al-Zaidi also directed that a joint investigative committee be formed with the relevant authorities in the Kurdish region to investigate the circumstances surrounding the attack, INA reported.
The attack comes amid heightened regional tensions. A drone strike hit the same facility last year, with no group having claimed responsibility.

articles.title_orig: 10 takeaways from Trump's 60 Minutes interview: Why GOP lost the midterms, what went wrong on immigration and more
articles.title_zh: 10 takeaways from Trump's 60 Minutes interview: Why GOP lost the midterms, what went wrong on immigration and more
articles.content_orig:
Days after Republicans faced a series of bruising midterm election losses, President Trump stood by his handling of the economy and the Iran war — but he acknowledged some "bad messaging" on economic issues and said his immigration crackdown was "too tough" at times.
In a sitdown with 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat, the president also suggested some top administration officials could be on their way out. One hour later, he announced White House chief of staff Susie Wiles would depart her role and be replaced by Stephen Miller.
Here are the biggest takeaways from the interview:
Republicans lost more than 40 House seats and at least seven Senate seats on Tuesday, with some races still uncalled, including in places that Mr. Trump won by double-digit margins two years ago. About 63% of midterm voters disapproved of Mr. Trump's job performance, and 44% said one reason for their vote was to express opposition to him, according to CBS News exit polling.
Asked for his analysis of the midterm losses, Mr. Trump told 60 Minutes that voters "didn't like the war" with Iran or the soaring gas prices that it triggered.
But he said he believes the primary reason for Republicans' losses was that "I was not on the ballot," an explanation he has offered several times in recent days. He suggested his pre-election endorsements and rallies "brought a lot of people … a lot closer to victory."
Ahead of Election Day, the president frequently urged his supporters to "pretend that I'm on the ballot." So, what happened?
"I think they didn't vote, really. I think they didn't vote. I think in some cases, they didn't like the candidates. And that's, you know, their prerogative," he said.
Some of the candidates were picked by the president. He endorsed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the Lone Star State's bitter GOP Senate primary, and he endorsed Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to fill her late brother's South Carolina Senate seat — encouraging her to run for a full term.
Mr. Trump argued that "Cornyn would have lost also."
The president defended his stewardship of the economy in his 60 Minutes sitdown, which came hours after a stronger-than-expected jobs report . He said "the numbers are phenomenal."
"We're doing numbers that have never been done before. 401(k)s are at their all-time high by a lot. Under other presidents, they were a disaster. 401(k)s have made people rich," the president said. Pressed on the fact that not all Americans have large retirement accounts, Mr. Trump responded: "But a lot of people do."
But exit polling shows three-fourths of midterm voters viewed the condition of the economy as either poor or not so good — and 70% of that group voted for Democratic House candidates. Voters were especially concerned about prices of gasoline, food, utilities and healthcare, and two-thirds of voters believed that Mr. Trump's tariff policies hurt the country's economy.
Mr. Trump said the problem is that "we couldn't get the word across."
"I think it was bad messaging, maybe by me, but I would talk about it all the time. So I don't know, how much can I talk about it?" the president said.
He predicted that Americans are "going to notice it in the next two, three, four months," arguing that his policies will lead to a resurgence of manufacturing jobs.
The morning after the election, Vice President JD Vance argued on social media "the real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone" — the broadly unpopular Iran war."
Mr. Trump said Vance told him about his plan to write that post, and he responded: "You write what you want." The president said "I don't disagree" with the vice president's diagnosis for why the Republicans lost the midterms, "other than one thing."
"The one thing he left out is — that I would say, and maybe he wouldn't say it, I don't know. I've never asked him really. But, if you had … to do again, would you do it? And that's Iran. Would you go and attack Iran?" he said.
The president said his answer to that question is an "emphatic yes," arguing Iran's conventional military has been degraded and its nuclear program has been set back.
"I think historically, this will be a very good decision. Is it a good decision for today and tomorrow? Maybe not? But … I have to go with what's right for our country," he said. "If they had a nuclear weapon during my term, I would be excoriated far worse than what's happened."
In a visit to the Oval Office later in the day, Mr. Trump reiterated his view that historians will judge the Iran war more favorably than voters. He pointed out a portrait of Ulysses S. Grant, a former president whose reputation has improved with age .
"I mean, he was very low on the list and now he's much higher on the list," Mr. Trump said. "I think as an example — the fact that I have taken the nuclear weapon away from Iran will not be good, short-term. But long-term, I think it's going to be very important."
Since September, Iran and the U.S. have largely held off from major attacks, though the U.S. launched a set of limited defensive strikes on Iranian targets earlier this week.
Mr. Trump has suggested in recent months that the war could ramp up again after the election, but he has also frequently predicted Iran is interested in striking a deal, and Qatar is mediating a diplomatic push between the two sides. He told 60 Minutes he believes Iran is close to striking a deal, but the outcome of the election "gives them a little bit of a hope certificate."
Asked if he plans to escalate the war now that the midterms are over, the president said: "Well, I'm not looking to. I don't think there's any reason to."
Mr. Trump's victory in 2024 was fueled in part by voters' discontent with the Biden administration's immigration policies. But this year, exit polling shows 58% think the Trump administration's actions on immigration have gone too far. In battlegrounds like Texas, many Latino voters who shifted to Mr. Trump two years ago pivoted back to Democrats due to concerns about immigration policy .
The president said immigration "both helped and hurt."
"I think I got an A+ for closing up the border," he said.
So, which immigration policies hurt him?
"For getting people out, I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out," Mr. Trump said. "But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally."
He continued: "Now, there is a large part of the country that think that they should be put out. And there's a large part of the country that think that they should be allowed to stay if they're good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes."
"I think it was too tough," the president said of his deportation policies.
Mr. Trump's plans for the second half of his term aren't clear. On Friday, he replaced White House chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller, a hardliner who is widely viewed as an architect of the Trump administration's immigration enforcement strategy. Last year, he pressed Immigration and Customs Enforcement to conduct at least 3,000 arrests per day .
The president said he'd "love to do something on immigration" with congressional Democrats.
Mr. Trump is the wealthiest person to hold the presidency, and his wealth has grown by billions in recent years, fueled partly by his family's cryptocurrency ventures . Polls show many voters believe the president is prioritizing his personal business interests while in office.
Asked about reporting by Forbes that his net worth has soared since he returned to the White House, Mr. Trump said, "So did everyone." (Douthat noted that, unlike Mr. Trump, his net worth hasn't gone up by nearly $3 billion. The president responded, "Well, you should've had stock.")

articles.title_orig: Chevy Blazer EV Police Cars Have Almost 500 HP And Are Used Performance Bargains
articles.title_zh: Chevy Blazer EV Police Cars Have Almost 500 HP And Are Used Performance Bargains
articles.content_orig:
True, most police cars don't come with V8 engines anymore, but that doesn't mean the cops have given up chasing people — which is unfortunate, since high-speed chases are dangerous for everyone . The difference is just that current police interceptors are now available with alternative forms of motivation. The 498-horsepower Chevrolet Blazer EV Police Pursuit Vehicle is a case in point: The second-quickest PPV in this year's Michigan State Police testing (PDF) – behind only the Mustang Mach-E GT eAWD — the Blazer is propelled by a pair of electric motors. And now that Chevy has been selling them to police departments for a couple of years, some are starting to come up on the used market. They're practically a steal, too, with examples listed below $30k on sites such as CarGurus , so you're getting a lot of horses for not a lot of money.
Among new cars, access to 500 horsepower will cost you at least about $25,000 more than that, regardless of powerplant. A gas-powered Dodge Charger Scat Pack, for instance, serves up 550 hp with an MSRP of $56,990 with destination. A Tesla Model 3 Performance, with 528 ponies, is listed at $56,630. Looking at the numbers based on price, the few new vehicles available under $30,000, such as the base model Honda Accord and Nissan Leaf, check in with 192 and 214 hp, respectively. One thing to keep in mind, though, is that the supply of used Chevy Blazer EV police cars is relatively limited. Only five were available nationwide on Carfax when this article was written, with prices ranging from $29,405 to $35,995.
The key distinction between the two comes down to the tuning of their powertrains. The EV PPV is based on the high-performance Blazer SS sold for retail customers. That's a machine we called a normal family crossover with supercar speed , thanks to its output of 615 hp and 650 lb-ft of torque. Of course, with great power comes great responsibility, which may be why the cops can't tap into all that output. Specific police tuning limits the Blazer EV PPV to 498 horsepower and 571 lb-ft. Still, the PPV is no slouch when it comes to acceleration and speed. Per testing with the Michigan State Police, it can reach 60 mph in a mere 5.14 seconds with a top speed of 130 mph.
And while that's a fairly large spread between the pre-owned police Blazers and the civilian range-toppers, the latter is also roughly twice the price. Chevrolet wants $62,495 for a 2027 Blazer SS EV with all-wheel drive after destination. The least expensive brand-new Blazer EV is $46,795 after destination.
Another important difference between the cop car and regular Blazer is that the former has a purpose-built electrical architecture with a 400- to 12-volt power module reducer and a universal vehicle module. These components help the Blazer PPV provide enough juice to power upfitter equipment and allow it to handle unique operation modes such as Shutdown Inhibit or Fast Idle. Also in the mix are front Brembo brakes, a heavy-duty suspension, and steel skid plates. And while some used examples still have bull bars attached, the red and blue flashing lights are not.

articles.title_orig: Saudi Aramco building in Riyadh damaged in ‘attempted’ attack
articles.title_zh: Saudi Aramco building in Riyadh damaged in ‘attempted’ attack
articles.content_orig:
A Saudi Aramco building in Riyadh has been damaged following an “attempted” attack, Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Energy said.
The administrative building was damaged by “falling shrapnel”, and there were no casualties, Saudi state media reported on Sunday, citing a senior source at the ministry.
Several news agencies reported that a tower belonging to the Saudi oil giant in the capital’s King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD) was damaged.
The reports came after the Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen’s Houthis said its air defences had destroyed several ballistic missiles launched by the Iran-aligned armed group towards the kingdom.
Two of the missiles were launched towards Riyadh, while another targeted the kingdom’s Eastern province, Major-General Turki al-Maliki, the coalition’s spokesperson, said in separate posts on X on Sunday.
The coalition also intercepted two missiles in the southern region, as well as a drone launched by the Houthis, al-Maliki said.
On Sunday, the Houthis claimed an attack on Saudi Aramco oil storage tanks, as well as on Riyadh’s King Khalid International airport. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group launched a second barrage against an Aramco facility in the city of Abqaiq.
Qatar, Bahrain, Egypt and Syria have condemned the attacks.
The Houthis have escalated attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia since a truce in Yemen’s war collapsed in July.
The group has also carried out attacks on King Fahd International airport in Dammam, the Ras Tanura and Rabigh oil refineries, and other airports across the kingdom.
At least 13 people were killed and more than 300 wounded in a Houthi strike on the Riyadh airport on October 10.
The attacks come as fighting intensifies across Yemen between the Houthis and government forces, who launched the Dawn of Yemen operation aimed at retaking Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, last month.
The spokesperson of the Houthi-run Health Ministry, Anees al-Asbahi, said on Saturday that 33 people, including eight women and 13 children, were killed after Saudi-led coalition air attacks on the village of al-Shariyah, near Sanaa.
In a post on X, al-Asbahi said at least 39 others were wounded in the attacks on Saturday, which targeted homes, roads, paramedics and civil defence teams in the village, located in the Bani Hushaish district east of Sanaa.
There was no immediate comment from the Saudi-led coalition on the reported strikes. Al Jazeera could not independently verify the reports.
Media outlets affiliated with the Houthis reported on Sunday that various areas of the Saada border district in Saada province have also been subjected to artillery shelling.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree earlier claimed that the coalition had carried out 105 air strikes and missile attacks over 24 hours targeting Sanaa and seven other governorates, taking the total number of strikes since the escalation began to 4,369.
On Friday, an attack on a market in Taiz province killed 30 people. The Houthis blamed it on the Saudi-led coalition, while Yemeni government forces accused the Houthis of firing a ballistic missile at the site.
According to the United Nations, more than 1,600 people have been killed and almost 300,000 displaced since a 2022 ceasefire collapsed in July, after the Houthis announced a blockade of Saudi ports.
In September, the Houthis seized much of Yemen’s Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive, while government forces launched a campaign to reclaim Houthi-held territory in October.

articles.title_orig: Rubio Warned Officials About Nvidia Chief’s Entanglement With Chinese Spy
articles.title_zh: Rubio Warned Officials About Nvidia Chief’s Entanglement With Chinese Spy
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang delivers his keynote on the company's GTC event in Berlin, Germany, Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. Markus Schreiber/AP hide caption
The massive artificial intelligence chip maker Nvidia says it is launching an internal investigation, after reports that the company's CEO was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.
In the statement announcing the investigation, Nvidia cited recent reporting by The New York Times , which alleges Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a Chinese intelligence operation that sought to send advanced Nvidia AI chips to China.
"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information," the statement from the company's board of directors reads in part.
The Times released a series of reports over the last two weeks detailing Huang's alleged relationship with a woman named Alice Huang, who is accused of being a spy for China. The two are not related. NPR has reached out to the Chinese Embassy in Washington, D.C. but has not received a response.
"Alice Huang is a Chinese national. She's a Chinese businesswoman who had something of a mysterious and meteoric rise," Times reporter Ana Swanson explained on NPR's technology podcast Machine Gods .
Alice Huang ran a Singapore-based company that purchased nearly $5 billion in Nvidia chip technology, Swanson says. "At the same time, she was also seen personally with Jensen Huang on a couple of occasions after some industry events in Taiwan. They were photographed together both at a bar with other suppliers and then also out to dinner with some other executives."
The reporting by the Times suggests Alice Huang may have helped China get around U.S. limits on exports of powerful AI chips.
According to Nvidia, Huang sent an email to his employees on Sunday, acknowledging the relationship, and apologizing for being unfaithful to his wife.
"I support the investigation and will cooperate fully," Huang wrote. "I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American."
Last week, three Republican members of Congress sent a letter to the Nvidia CEO requesting that he brief lawmakers about the relationship, and about the company's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage."
Nvidia dominates the global market for AI chips, and has seen explosive growth in recent years, as NPR has reported . The company started as a manufacturer of chips for computer graphics, which later turned out to be crucial for training artificial intelligence .
Nvidia's CEO and President Trump have repeatedly appeared in public together in recent years. According to Huang, Nvidia is helping to fund the construction of a new ballroom at the White House.
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

articles.title_orig: In 1984 After He Bought Her Company, Warren Buffett Said He'd "Rather Wrestle Grizzlies Than Compete With Mrs. B And Her Progeny." Five Years Later Rose Blumkin Opened A Rival Store Across The Street. In 1992 Buffett Bought It Too - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.title_zh: In 1984 After He Bought Her Company, Warren Buffett Said He'd "Rather Wrestle Grizzlies Than Compete With Mrs. B And Her Progeny." Five Years Later Rose Blumkin Opened A Rival Store Across The Street. In 1992 Buffett Bought It Too - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.content_orig:
Rose Blumkin arrived in America penniless, spoke no English, and built a retail empire that Warren Buffett paid millions to own. Then she walked away angry, and Buffett learned what happens when you forget to lock down a legend.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Warren Buffett has a favorite test for sizing up a business, and he spelled it out in the Berkshire Hathaway ( NYSE:BRK-A | BRK-A Price Prediction ) ( NYSE:BRK-B ) 1983 shareholder letter , dated March 14, 1984: “One question I always ask myself in appraising a business is how I would like, assuming I had ample capital and skilled personnel, to compete with it. I’d rather wrestle grizzlies than compete with Mrs. B and her progeny.” Berkshire had closed its purchase of Nebraska Furniture Mart in 1983, and the letter’s earnings table shows the store only from October through December. Five years later, Rose Blumkin ran that test herself.
Warren Buffett wrote that about 67 years earlier, Mrs. Blumkin, then 23, “talked her way past a border guard to leave Russia for America.” She “had no formal education, not even at the grammar school level, and knew no English.” Warren Buffett told that after years of selling used clothing, she had saved $500 by 1937 to open a furniture store. By the time of the letter, Warren Buffett wrote, Nebraska Furniture Mart generated over $100 million in annual sales from one store.
Her discounting once landed her in court over Fair Trade pricing. Buffett’s account of the verdict: “After demonstrating to the court that she could profitably sell carpet at a huge discount from the prevailing price, she sold the judge $1400 worth of carpet.”
Warren Buffett wrote in 1983 that Berkshire bought 90% of the business, leaving 10% with family members involved in management. His 1992 letter says the family sold 80% in 1983, so the two letters give different figures. Warren Buffett added that Mrs. B, “now 90,” “remains Chairman and is on the sales floor seven days a week.”
She kept going. In the 1986 letter, Warren Buffett wrote that Mrs. B “continues at age 93 to outsell and out-hustle any manager I’ve ever seen.” He added: “Competing with her represents a triumph of courage over judgment.” Mrs. B soon tested that line herself.
Buffett’s 1989 letter, dated March 2, 1990, reported that Mrs. B quit in May after a disagreement with the family over the carpet department. Buffett wrote: “At age 96 she has started a new business selling (what else?) carpet and furniture.” He also wrote: “Mrs. B probably has made more smart business decisions than any living American.”
Wikipedia, citing the New York Times, reports that she came out of retirement within three months to open Mrs. B’s Warehouse directly across the street, and that it turned profitable by 1991. Buffett’s 1992 letter places it next door, in a building she owned. The accounts differ on exact position. Either way, she had never signed a non-compete.
Buffett’s 1992 letter, dated March 1, 1993, says that at the end of 1992 Mrs. B decided to sell her building and land to Nebraska Furniture Mart, which set up shop alongside her in that building. “I am delighted that Mrs. B has again linked up with us,” he wrote. The buyer was Berkshire’s Nebraska Furniture Mart, and the deal covered her building and land, plus a non-compete she “graciously offered to sign.”
The division that houses Nebraska Furniture Mart remains a profit engine. In Q2 2026, manufacturing, service and retailing operating earnings grew to $4.47B from $3.60B a year earlier, while total operating earnings rose to $12.98B from $11.16B, per Berkshire’s August 8-K filing. Greg Abel now runs the company as CEO. Class B shares have gained 14.18% year to date and trade at a P/E of about 12. Investors watching the third-quarter earnings report should keep an eye on whether that segment’s momentum holds.
Buffett’s 1992 letter closed the story with his own comment: “Mrs. B belongs in the Guinness Book of World Records on many counts. Signing a non-compete at 99 merely adds one more.” According to J. Weekly, Rose Blumkin died in 1998 at 104. She was the immigrant who started with savings from selling used clothes, outsold every manager Buffett knew, and was the only competitor he ever said he would rather wrestle grizzlies than face.

AJ spent 10 years writing about financial markets at The Motley Fool. His coverage centers on technology stocks and the broader macroeconomic trends, from interest rates to geopolitics,  that shape where markets are headed next. AJ is drawn to the stories where big-picture economics and individual companies collide.

articles.title_orig: Elon Musk sends a strong signal to SpaceX stock investors
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk sends a strong signal to SpaceX stock investors
articles.content_orig:
Musk hinted at a telecom takeover without naming a target, while a rival CEO put a staggering price on SpaceX's ambitions. Debt, regulators, and a spectrum gap stand between the boast and a real deal.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Elon Musk told investors on November 6, 2026, that SpaceX ( NASDAQ:SPCX | SPCX Price Prediction ) could buy a legacy telecom carrier and use its airwaves “ten times more effectively.” He made the comment by video with Ron Baron at the annual Baron Investment Conference in New York.
Musk also said SpaceX could go far with the spectrum it already has, and he named no target. He made any purchase conditional on SpaceX using spectrum better than the incumbent does.
T-Mobile ( NASDAQ:TMUS ) rose 0.88%. Verizon ( NYSE:VZ ) and AT&T ( NYSE:T ) each slipped 0.89%. SpaceX rose 8.62% to $134.27, but Musk also gave his revenue outlook in the same conversation, and the stock had lost 19.89% over the prior month during a post-election Nasdaq rout .
Spectrum means licensed radio frequencies. A phone can connect to a satellite or a tower only on airwaves the operator has the legal right to use, so those licenses determine whether direct-to-phone service can work at scale.
SpaceX bought AWS-4 and H-block licenses from EchoStar on September 8, 2025, for roughly $17 billion. It paid $8.5 billion in cash and $8.5 billion in SpaceX stock. It has also agreed to buy nationwide 800 MHz licenses, with closing expected in the first half of 2027. There are also reports of talks over Boost Mobile, but nothing has been confirmed.
On Deutsche Telekom’s November 5 earnings call, CEO Tim Hoettges said SpaceX would need at least EUR 200 billion, or about $220 billion, to compete with the established US carriers. His company controls T-Mobile, so he has a reason to make entry look expensive.
He put SpaceX’s spectrum at 76 MHz, compared with roughly 400 MHz for T-Mobile. He said leasing tower space alone would cost $20 billion to $30 billion, but he still said his company has to assume SpaceX will enter the market.
At the close, the three carriers were worth about $507 billion combined. SpaceX was worth roughly $1.77 trillion, so a deal paid partly in stock is possible on paper.
A buyer would also take on debt, including Verizon’s $166.2 billion or AT&T’s $159.6 billion, along with labor unions, retail stores and landline networks. Antitrust regulators and the FCC would both have to approve it.
T-Mobile is down 18.46% year to date, and its third-quarter report pointed to worry over SpaceX’s fourth-carrier ambitions. Verizon closed at $45.71 and AT&T at $21.63. No one linked their small moves to Musk.
Viasat ( NASDAQ:VSAT ) rose 7.7% to $63.95 after its results. Its CFO said Viasat ended the quarter with 100,000 US fixed broadband subscribers paying $111 a month on average, and fixed services revenue fell 23%.
Investor Sawyer Merritt noted that Viasat had 603,000 subscribers in September 2020, the year Starlink opened to the public. That is a drop of 83%, which shows Starlink is already pulling customers from older satellite providers.
At $134.27, SpaceX’s price likely already assumes Starlink Mobile succeeds. Turning Musk’s comment into a carrier business would bring debt, regulators, and a bill that Hoettges puts at $220 billion or more.
T-Mobile’s recent results give a useful point of comparison. It raised its 2026 Core Adjusted EBITDA guidance to $37.35 billion to $37.45 billion and raised its dividend 15% to $1.17 a share, and its stock price already reflects the fear of SpaceX.
Keep an eye on the 800 MHz closing in the first half of 2027. If no SpaceX filing with the FCC or SEC names a US carrier by then, the comment is still just a hypothetical, and T-Mobile’s discount should narrow.

articles.title_orig: 60 Minutes Transcript: Donald Trump, the 2026 post-midterm elections interview
articles.title_zh: 60 Minutes Transcript: Donald Trump, the 2026 post-midterm elections interview
articles.content_orig:
This past Tuesday, President Donald Trump's Republican Party suffered an extraordinary midterm repudiation – losing not just the House and Senate, but statewide offices in red states, from Texas to Kansas to South Carolina, that Democrats hadn't won in decades. In the past, this president has met defeat with claims of fraud and the effort to overturn the 2020 election. But when we met with him in the White House on Friday for his first sit-down interview since the midterms, we found him in a surprisingly reflective mood, and seemingly accepting of defeat. Our wide-ranging conversation covered: immigration and corruption, Iran and artificial intelligence, his potential successors and his own mortality. But we began with the election results.
Ross Douthat: Two years ago, you won a big, some might say historic, victory. Just now, the Republican party in the midterms suffered a big, some might say, historic defeat. Give me your political analysis of what just happened.
President Donald Trump: Well, number one, I was not on the ballot. But I campaigned hard for some people. And-- I think if I was on the ballot, it would've been a much different situation because you saw the level of popularity and love. There was love. We had massive rallies. You had to transfer those voters, however, to candidates that they didn't like. But there's something beyond that. They didn't like the war. They didn't like the fact that gasoline went up, 'cause I had it down at a low, and there's-- a great dislike, incredibly, for Israel.
Ross Douthat: Let's go through those then one by one.
President Donald Trump: Go ahead.
Ross Douthat: Start-- start with the candidates, right? You said it was tough to transfer your own appeal to candidates
President Donald Trump: Yeah.
Ross Douthat: But in a lot of cases, you picked the candidates. You endorsed Ken Paxton--
President Donald Trump: Well, I--
President Donald Trump: I--
Ross Douthat: He had a tough time.
President Donald Trump: Sure.
Ross Douthat: You endorsed Darline Graham--
President Donald Trump: But-- but Cornyn--
Ross Douthat: --in South Carolina.
President Donald Trump: --Cornyn would've lost also. Darline, I did that in-- honor of a man named Lindsey, who was a friend of mine. And she fought hard. She fought hard. She really did.
Ross Douthat: She lost a very Republican state.
President Donald Trump: Oh--
Ross Douthat: To a very liberal challenger--
President Donald Trump: I won-- I won South Carolina by the highest vote in history by far. I won Texas by the highest vote in history by far. I won Florida who, by the way, I did endorse. And he's gonna be-- a great governor and a great senator. I endorsed both of them. And, had I not endorsed them, they wouldn't have won.
Ross Douthat: Why can't it transfer? You-- you were out on the trail, and you said--
President Donald Trump: It didn't transfer--
Ross Douthat: You said, "Vote like I'm on the ballot."
President Donald Trump: Yeah. It didn't--
Ross Douthat: And people didn't? Or-- or did they? Did they vote because they were mad at you--
President Donald Trump: No, they--
President Donald Trump: I think they didn't vote, really. I think in some cases, they didn't like the candidates. And that's, you know, their prerogative.
Ross Douthat: Couple days ago your vice president, JD Vance, wrote a social media post where he says, "The reason we lost is the war," meaning Iran. And he said things in that post--
President Donald Trump: I don't disagree--
Ross Douthat: About Israel. Yeah. So you agree with his analysis?
President Donald Trump: I don't disagree with it
Ross Douthat: Did you know he was gonna write that post?
President Donald Trump: He asked me what do I think. I said, "You write what you're--" I said--
Ross Douthat: "Write what you--"
President Donald Trump: You write what you want--"
Ross Douthat: "Write what you feel"?
President Donald Trump: By the way, "What are you gonna write? "The only thing I wish he would've said there, if he felt it, and you'd have to ask him about that, but if you had to do it again, would you do it? You know, he's part of a decision-making process. And my answer is an emphatic yes because you can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon. I think, historically, this will be a very good decision. Is it a good decision for today and tomorrow? Maybe not. But you know, I have to go with what's right for our country. If they had a nuclear weapon during my term, I would be excoriated far worse than what's happened. So--
Ross Douthat: All right. Let's-- let's--
President Donald Trump: I've stopped--
President Donald Trump: But Ross, I've stopped them from having a nuclear weapon. That's a big thing.
The president argued that even with the Iran war, the U.S. economy in his second term has been very strong.
Ross Douthat: But in poll after poll, people say they're unhappy with this economy in a way they weren't in the first term. Cost of living, inflation, and so on. Is that all just the Iran war?
President Donald Trump: Well, it's not really the Iran war because the numbers are phenomenal. I think it was bad messaging, maybe by me, but I would talk about it all the time. So I don't know, how much can I talk about it? Look, the press doesn't cover-- positive news for Republicans. They don't cover certainly positive news for me. So I have to do it myself. I have to get it out there. We have historically good numbers. We have the highest stock market in history.
Ross Douthat: But why don't Americans feel it, that--
President Donald Trump: They don't--
Ross Douthat: Why-- why don't they-- 'cause they're--
President Donald Trump: Because I think--
Ross Douthat: Obviously, like, you and the press, you and the media, you and our business have been in tension throughout your career.
President Donald Trump: Correct.
Ross Douthat: But you still won elections, right?
President Donald Trump: Yeah.
Ross Douthat: So why couldn't you win this time--
President Donald Trump: I think it was bad messaging.
Ross Douthat: What was the bad message?
President Donald Trump: We couldn't get the word across.
Whether it was the message or the record, the Republican collapse will give Democrats in Congress new powers over budgets, hearings, and subpoenas.
Ross Douthat: You came out after the midterms. You congratulated the Democrats.
President Donald Trump: Correct.
Ross Douthat: You said that you were open to working with them.
President Donald Trump: True.
Ross Douthat: What is one thing you would like to work with a Democratic majority on--
President Donald Trump: I'd love to do something on immigration.
President Donald Trump: Because-- well, so
Ross Douthat: Do you think immigration hurt you in the midterms?
President Donald Trump: I think--
Ross Douthat: Do you think the crackdown hurt you--
President Donald Trump: I think it both helped and hurt. I think I got an A+ for closing up the border. I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out. But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that-- that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally. Now, there is a large part of the country that think that they should be put out. And there's a large part of the country that think that they should be allowed to stay if they're good people working in a landscaping company, or workin' in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes. And there's a large group of people who think that they should be allowed to stay.
Ross Douthat: So you think your deportation policy--
President Donald Trump: I think it was--
Ross Douthat: Went too far--
President Donald Trump: Too tough.
Ross Douthat: It was too tough?
President Donald Trump: I think it might be too tough, yeah.
Ross Douthat: What would--
President Donald Trump: And-- and I think--
Ross Douthat: What does a deal look like
President Donald Trump: I think ultimately--
Ross Douthat: With the Democrats?
President Donald Trump: That hurt me. We

articles.title_orig: Oil falls as Trump says new Iran attacks 'unlikely'
articles.title_zh: Oil falls as Trump says new Iran attacks 'unlikely'
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices on Friday posted a steep weekly loss, as investors weighed the risk of renewed military escalation between the U.S. and Iran following the midterm elections.
International benchmark Brent crude futures added 3 cents to close at $98.32 per barrel. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures gained 31 cents to settle at $90.83 per barrel. Brent fell more than 16% for the week while U.S. crude lost neary 13%.
Investors are assessing whether the conclusion of the U.S. midterm elections could pave the way for renewed actions against Iran, potentially threatening oil supplies from the Middle East.
Bob McNally, Rapidan Energy Group founder and president, told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" that he sees an 80% probability of military fighting resuming, forecasting that both oil benchmarks could climb above $100 a barrel.
However, hopes for a diplomatic resolution have also emerged after Iran reportedly sent a nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatar, Reuters reported, citing a senior Iranian official.
Iran reported three additional attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, while data from the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) indicated that attacks on vessels were continuing at a near-record rate.
"President Donald Trump is determined, as a legacy item, almost at all costs, to prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon, having them give up their nuclear capabilities," McNally said.
"The Iranian regime, on the other hand, is not willing to do it. And as long as that core difference in that deal space is absent, the escalation dynamic remains in place," he added.
McNally's view is shared by other analysts, including Lombard Odier's chief economist Samy Chaar and head of investment strategy Luca Bindelli.
— CNBC's Lim Hui Jie contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s proposed Russia deal raises NATO alarm as ex-commander warns Putin seeks influence over Europe
articles.title_zh: Trump’s proposed Russia deal raises NATO alarm as ex-commander warns Putin seeks influence over Europe
articles.content_orig:
Retired Gen. Philip Breedlove warns any deal meeting Russia's demands could face European resistance.
President Donald Trump's push for a deal with Russia to end the war in Ukraine and potentially reshape European security has raised alarm among NATO allies, with a former top alliance commander warning Fox News Digital that President Vladimir Putin has long sought to divide the world into competing spheres of influence.
The warning came as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also appeared to reject what he called a potential "Yalta 2.0," and NATO allies debated direct outreach to Putin ahead of delegations preparing for talks in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11.
Retired Gen. Philip Breedlove , the former Supreme Allied Commander Europe, warned that Putin's ambitions extend far beyond Ukraine and reflect a broader vision for how global powers should divide influence.
"Putin has a plan for the world, and he has pushed that plan on leaders several times," Breedlove warned before adding: "He talks about it and he writes about it."
ZELENSKYY TO SEEK OFFRAMP FOR YEARS-LONG RUSSIA WAR IN UN SPEECH AFTER TRUMP REVEALS PEACE DEAL IS CLOSE
Finnish President Alexander Stubb, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, French President Emmanuel Macron, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, front row from left, and Jonas Gahr Støre, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, Ursula von der Leyen, Dutch Prime Minister Dick Schoof, and Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, back row from left, stand together in the chancellery in Berlin, Germany, on Dec. 15, 2025. (Markus Schreiber, Pool/AP)
Trump had suggested Thursday that an agreement with Moscow could extend beyond ending Russia's nearly five-year war in Ukraine.
"It's going to be a big agreement, and it's going to involve more than Ukraine... I could even say it might involve all of Europe," Trump told reporters after meeting Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev at the White House.
"It's going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone's going to be thrilled," Trump added.
Breedlove said Putin has repeatedly promoted a vision of dividing global power among Russia, China and the United States.
"The plan is three spheres of influence whereby China controls the Far East, Russia controls Europe, and America controls the Western Hemisphere. I do not expect there's going to be a lot of cooperation from the countries of Europe," he said.
"The Western world is waiting to see what this big plan is, and they are very concerned because it is about them," Breedlove added.
President Donald Trump (R) and Russian President Vladimir Putin (L) hold a meeting at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson on August 15, 2025 in Anchorage, Alaska. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
Zelenskyy also warned Friday against repeating the 1945 Yalta Conference , where Allied leaders negotiated Europe's postwar order before the Soviet Union consolidated control over Eastern Europe.
"We don't want to have Yalta 2.0," the Ukrainian leader told CNN . "We don't want to be divided by Russia," he said before adding: "For me, it's not simple and it can be dangerous."
On Sunday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters that discussions on how Europe would look after the Ukraine war were already underway.
"It's one of the key topics that's been raised repeatedly in every conversation, anytime negotiations have been discussed," he said ahead of traveling to Paris for the G7 meeting.
RUBIO SOUNDS CAMPAIGN-READY AS HE RAILS AGAINST OPEN BORDERS, GLOBALISM IN SPEECH FROM ANCIENT GREEK RUINS
Secretary of State Marco Rubio talks to reporters at NATO Headquarters in Brussels, Belgium, on Friday, April 4. (Jacquelyn Martin/Pool/AP)
"So I think that's what the president is alluding to, is that there's been some advances made and what that architecture could look like post-conflict. We obviously have to get past the conflict to get to that point," he added, clarifying Trump's comments.
Breedlove, however, questioned whether European governments and Ukraine would even accept a broader agreement negotiated without their involvement.
"I do expect that when we get a peek under the hood of what Mr. Putin and Mr. Trump have devised that there may be European partners and allies to include Ukraine that may or may not be enthralled with the proposed solution."
"We have always said nothing about Ukraine without Ukraine," the expert said.
"Neither have we heard anything about the EU or NATO being in this conversation. And yet the EU, NATO and Ukraine are central and the heart of the matter that apparently is going to be discussed."
Tensions also appeared to mount further after Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre held a rare 90-minute telephone conversation with Putin on Oct. 27, according to reports .
TRUMP NEGOTIATORS WITKOFF, KUSHNER MEET WITH PUTIN IN MOSCOW AS US PUSHES FOR END TO RUSSIA-UKRAINE WAR
A composite image shows Russian President Vladimir Putin (L) and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy (R) as peace talks continue. (Valery Sharifulin/Pool/AFP via Getty Images; Sean Gallup/Getty Images)
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen criticized the separate European diplomatic initiatives.
"I think Europe should stick together rather than going solo," she said as Breedlove went on to defend the outreach.
"The two calls that recently took place between Northern leaders in the NATO alliance and Russia, I don't think that they're out of place at all," he said. "I think they're entirely appropriate."
"The great powers of Europe are getting very concerned that someone is dealing with their security without including them in the conversation," he added.
Meanwhile, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot confirmed Sunday that France would participate in the Abu Dhabi negotiations.
"The Europeans will be well represented; France will be in Abu Dhabi to take part in these discussions," Barrot said, according to Reuters.
FORMER UK PRIME MINISTER TONY BLAIR WARNS EUROPE ‘WE DON’T WIN’ IN WAR WITHOUT US SUPPORT
President Donald Trump speaks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, as they meet to negotiate for an end to the war in Ukraine, at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson in Anchorage, Alaska, U.S., August 15, 2025. (Kevin Lamarque/Reuters)
Breedlove warned that any agreement requiring European nations to sacrifice their security to satisfy Moscow would still face fierce resistance.
"If the maximalist demands of Russia remain intact and in order to find peace, all the rest of Europe has to give up its security, sacrifice its security, make itself more susceptible to Russian attack, then this is not going to go well," he said.
"Putin has never been a partner for peace in Ukraine. Putin is not now a partner for peace in Ukraine."
"The EU nations, the NATO nations, and Ukraine are not going to sign up to a plan that suggests that Russia will be able to once again amass its armies, march across borders and intervene in its neighbors' internal business."

"We need to understand that we are in a war. Mr. Putin is at war with the West," he warned.
Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.
