articles.title_orig: Will Eisenkot be able to form Israel’s next gov’t amid divided opposition?
articles.title_zh: Will Eisenkot be able to form Israel’s next gov’t amid divided opposition?
articles.content_orig:
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has been given the opportunity to form a new government after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s ruling coalition lost its parliamentary majority in the October elections, raising the possibility of an end to his long tenure in power.
President Isaac Herzog selected the former military chief on Saturday, following consultations with political parties. Eisenkot has 28 days to cobble together a coalition to form a government. If he fails to form a new administration within that period, he can seek a 14-day extension.
“Now is the time to form a national emergency government. I will do everything to ensure we are worthy,” Eisenkot, the leader of the Yashar party, posted on X.
However, the 66-year-old faces a difficult challenge as many of the opposition parties hold sharply conflicting positions on national security, religion and the Israeli occupation of Palestinian territory.
Neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu has a 61-seat majority in Israel’s 120-member parliament, the Knesset.
As a result, Arab-led parties hold a potentially decisive role in determining who governs Israel, even as Eisenkot and his prospective partners refuse to rely on their support.
So what do we now know about Eisenkot’s possible paths to power, and can he succeed in unseating Netanyahu?
Eisenkot’s potential coalition spans his Yashar party, the centre-left Democrats led by Yair Golan, Naftali Bennett’s centre-right Together party and Avigdor Lieberman’s right-wing Yisrael Beiteinu (Israel Our Home).
Overall, they control 48 seats, well short of a majority.
Arab-led parties Ra’am (United List) and the Joint List (comprising three parties – Hadash, Ta’al and Balad) – jointly holding 19 seats – have endorsed Eisenkot’s attempt to form a government. Their backing would give the broader anti-Netanyahu camp a combined 67 seats.
Hadash is an Arab-Jewish party, Ta’al advocates for the rights of Palestinian citizens of Israel, and Balad demands equal rights for all its citizens.
However, Eisenkot has ruled out bringing Arab parties into his government, while Lieberman has repeatedly rejected forming a minority administration dependent on their support. Golan’s Democrats have been more willing to partner with Ra’am and the Joint List.
“We must no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes,” Golan said after the election.
Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist coalition has fallen from the 64 seats it secured in 2022 to 53, eight seats short of a majority.
His Likud is the largest individual party with 27 seats, while Eisenkot’s Yashar won 21.
Netanyahu’s efforts to remain in power suffered a further setback when United Torah Judaism, a longtime ultra-Orthodox ally, declined to endorse him or any other candidate during consultations with Herzog.
While the decision hurts Netanyahu’s prospects of regaining power, it did not rule out the party supporting him in future coalition negotiations if their demands were met, particularly compulsory military service for ultra-Orthodox Jews, which they reject.
If Eisenkot is unable to put together a coalition, he could potentially lead a minority government backed by Arab parties from outside.
A minority government is formed when the parties holding cabinet positions do not collectively control a majority of seats in parliament. Instead, they depend on support from lawmakers outside the governing coalition to remain in power and pass legislation.
Eisenkot could establish such an administration with his four-party bloc relying on external parliamentary support from Ra’am and the Joint List .
Under this arrangement, the Arab-led parties would not necessarily receive cabinet positions or formally join the coalition.
They could instead negotiate policy concessions in exchange for their parliamentary support.
In 2021, Ra’am joined a government led by Bennett, becoming the first independent Arab party to participate in an Israeli governing coalition.
That administration collapsed after 18 months, mainly due to disagreements over the illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and Palestinian statehood. Most Israeli parties do not support the creation of a sovereign Palestinian state as part of the so-called two-state solution.
Netanyahu, who has been in power for most of the past 20 years, has openly rejected Palestinian statehood and has pushed settlement expansions that are the biggest hurdles in the realisation of Palestinian statehood. Settlements are considered illegal under international law.
Beyond a minority government, Eisenkot could attempt to secure a parliamentary majority by bringing Israel’s two ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism, into his coalition.
Together, they hold 13 seats, which would give Eisenkot’s bloc exactly the 61 seats required for a majority.
However, such an alliance would require compromises over military conscription exemptions for ultra-Orthodox religious students, an issue that has long divided Israeli politics.
Eisenkot and his allies, particularly Lieberman, have criticised the exemptions. But Lieberman has recently indicated that he is open to compromise.
While United Torah Judaism has refused to endorse Netanyahu, Shas backed the beleaguered prime minister.
Another option would be a unity government involving Eisenkot’s Yashar, Bennett’s Together party, Lieberman’s Israel Our Home and Netanyahu’s Likud.
Such an alliance would command 67 seats, but would require Eisenkot and his partners to abandon their central election pledge to remove Netanyahu from power.
If Eisenkot fails to form a government within the required time, Herzog could give Netanyahu an opportunity to form a governing coalition.
Should both leaders fail, parliament could nominate another candidate. If no government emerges after a process lasting 100 days, Israelis could be heading to the polls again.
The negotiations could determine not only who becomes Israel’s next prime minister, but also which political parties control key ministries and shape policies on the economy, military conscription and the occupied Palestinian territory.
Several members of Eisenkot’s opposition bloc have previously held senior government positions, including in the coalition that removed Netanyahu from power in 2021.
Bennett, who served as prime minister from 2021 to 2022, has long opposed the establishment of a Palestinian state and advocated annexing large parts of the occupied West Bank.
During Israel’s 11-day war on Gaza in May 2021, Bennett, then an opposition politician, backed Netanyahu’s military offensive in the Palestinian enclave. More than 250 Palestinians were killed in Israeli attacks.
Meanwhile, Lieberman served as finance minister in Bennett’s government and previously held the defence portfolio under Netanyahu.
He previously proposed swapping some Arab communities in Israel proper for Jewish settlements in the occupied West Bank in the context of a final peace deal with the Palestinians.
Lieberman’s party backs illegal settlement expansion, including E1, and annexing all of Area C, 60 percent of the occupied West Bank already under full Israeli control. E1, which stands for East 1 settlement, is a 12sq km corridor with thousands of housing units. It will cut the West Bank into two parts.
Eisenkot himself served in Netanyahu’s wartime cabinet before leaving the government after disagreements over the conduct of the genocide in Gaza. He has not opposed the genocide but criticised Netanyahu for prioritising his political survival over security considerations.
He has called the idea of a Palestinian state “delusional”, and he supports “strengthening” illegal settlements.
Academic Neve Gordon says an Eisenkot government could bring notable changes to Israel’s domestic politics, particularly by reversing parts of Netanyahu’s judicial overhaul.

articles.title_orig: South Africa’s ANC suffers setback in local elections
articles.title_zh: South Africa’s ANC suffers setback in local elections
articles.content_orig:
South Africa’s African National Congress (ANC) party faces a major setback after last week’s municipal elections, leaving it in a weak position in coalition talks to form city governments.
With all votes counted on Sunday, President Cyril Ramaphosa’s ANC had just over 30 percent nationally against about 25 percent for its main rival, the Democratic Alliance (DA).
That represents a drop of roughly 14 percentage points from its 2021 local elections performance.
Former President Jacob Zuma’s uMkhonto weSizwe party won about 10 percent of votes, putting it in third place, while the rest of the ballots were split between hundreds of smaller parties.
While still the largest party in South Africa, the ANC’s support has steadily eroded as voters grow increasingly frustrated with corruption and the party’s failure to tackle unemployment, which tops 34 percent more than three decades after the end of apartheid.
Failures in basic services, such as water and electricity, have also contributed to the ANC’s vote share falling in local elections over the past 15 years.
The party failed to win an outright majority in any of the eight major metro areas, including Johannesburg and Pretoria.
Since no party won more than 50 percent of the votes in many cities, including South Africa’s commercial hub Johannesburg, the ANC and DA will have to team up or hash it out with smaller parties to form municipal governments.
Parties will have 14 days to negotiate before city councils are formed.
ANC Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula called the result “catastrophic” for the ANC but said the party would not go begging for positions when coalition talks begin soon.
“When the people tell us we have fallen short, … the honest answer is not to argue with them but to go home and put our house in order,” Mbalula said on Saturday.
In Johannesburg, the DA led the count with about 35 percent of the votes, compared with 20 percent for the ANC.
That could give DA veteran Helen Zille, who campaigned on fixing potholes and leaking water pipes, a good chance of becoming mayor, depending on the coalition agreements reached.
The DA said in a statement that it would initiate coalition discussions with “political parties that share a commitment to clean and accountable government, rooting out corruption, service delivery for all, the rule of law, and non-racialism”.

articles.title_orig: CEO SUNDAY: Army veteran turned health tech boss calls support for those who served a 'sacred obligation'
articles.title_zh: CEO SUNDAY: Army veteran turned health tech boss calls support for those who served a 'sacred obligation'
articles.content_orig:
Philips North America CEO Jeff DiLullo shares how his Army service shaped his leadership, career and commitment to supporting veterans.
Long after Jeff DiLullo traded his Army uniform for a suit, a lesson from his years at West Point and in the military has stayed with him: the importance of serving "something bigger" than himself.
As CEO of Philips North America, a global health technology company that makes medical equipment used in hospitals, DiLullo has found a new way to put that lesson into practice through his work supporting veterans and their families.
"One of the most rewarding things for me personally that I've brought from my military service into my corporate life is a sense of service and serving something bigger than myself," DiLullo told FOX Business. "And now today, I do that through serving our veteran community."
BUILT FROM SCRATCH: HOW A RENTED KITCHEN AND HAND-SQUEEZED FRUIT BECAME A VERSATILE MIXER
He added, "To me, it's a sacred obligation as a nation to serve our veterans and not only them, but their families and caregivers too."
DiLullo graduated from the United States Military Academy at West Point with a bachelor's degree in history before serving as an infantry officer in the U.S. Army. He later earned an MBA in marketing , logistics and supply chain from the University of Tennessee's Haslam College of Business.
GOOGLE PARTNERS WITH VETERANS GROUPS TO HELP 25,000 ENTER SKILLED TRADES CAREERS AMID WORKER SHORTAGE
As CEO of Philips North America, DiLullo has found a new way to put that lesson into practice through his work supporting veterans and their families. (Philips North America)
His connection to military service has only become more personal in recent years. DiLullo's daughter and son-in-law are both currently on active duty, and he knows firsthand that eventually leaving the military can bring its own challenges.
"When you leave the military, you wonder if you're going to maintain the connection to a mission and something important and purposeful," DiLullo said. "Many veterans struggle with that transition just like I did."
After leaving the Army, he built a successful career in corporate America, eventually holding executive leadership positions at Hewlett-Packard, Avaya and Dell.
"After the Army, honestly, I buried myself in work," he said. "I tried to find a sense of purpose and mission in what I was doing, and I had great jobs, but I hit a wall, and I was trying to do everything well but not feeling that I was really deeply connected to my own sense of purpose."
The realization ultimately pushed him to rethink what he wanted from his career.
"After a period of reflection, almost 10 years ago, I decided to just change course completely," he said. "I moved into healthcare and I decided I would only work where I felt a personal sense of purpose, and I have never looked back. I'm having the most fun I've had in my entire career."
VETERAN-OWNED TEA COMPANY AIMS TO HELP FORMER SERVICE MEMBERS ‘FIND PURPOSE’
DiLullo joined Philips in 2019 as head of North America operations.
That path eventually brought DiLullo to Philips, where he joined the company in 2019 as head of North America operations. His responsibilities expanded in 2021 to include leadership of the company's North America services and solutions delivery teams.
Today, DiLullo said his work has given him a renewed connection to the sense of mission he valued in the military.
The Department of Veterans Affairs is Philips' largest customer , according to DiLullo, and he also serves on the board of the Elizabeth Dole Foundation, which supports military and veteran caregivers.
"These things are fuel for me and really fuel my sense of purpose and connection and service," he said.
Asked what advice he would offer today's West Point cadets, DiLullo said their commitment to the country does not have to end when their military careers do.
"You've taken a solemn vow to serve and defend your nation ," he said. "You have willingly taken up the responsibility to protect the freedoms that are the foundation of this great country."
DiLullo added, "Service does not end when you leave the military. Your oath is to a lifetime of service to the nation. So my advice will be always to know and serve something bigger than yourself."
VETERANS ARE USING THIS HOMEBUYING BENEFIT MORE OFTEN — BUT MANY STILL DON’T KNOW IT EXISTS
DiLullo graduated from the United States Military Academy at West Point with a bachelor's degree in history before serving as an infantry officer in the U.S. Army. (Rich Graessle/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)
Among all the roles DiLullo has held since leaving the military, one still stands apart.
CLICK HERE TO GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO
"I can honestly say, other than the military, this is the most fulfilling work I've ever done," he said of his work in healthcare.
But the best job he ever had?
"The best job I ever had was the Army," DiLullo said. "A sense of mission, teamwork, and trust. It just defined my ideal world."

articles.title_orig: Asia Power Snapshot: China, the United States, and the race for AI dominance
articles.title_zh: Asia Power Snapshot: China, the United States, and the race for AI dominance
articles.content_orig:
Subscribe to The Informer for monthly expert analysis, and to Events for advance notice of visiting world leaders and distinguished guests.
You may unsubscribe from Lowy Institute newsletters at any time. For information on our privacy practices and how to unsubscribe, see our Privacy Policy .
Who is winning the AI race between the United States and China? The answer depends on what you measure.
Photo: Jason Edwards/Getty
Asia Power Snapshot: China, the United States, and the race for AI dominance
US President Donald Trump has declared that “whoever wins AI wins,” suggesting that the competition for mastery over artificial intelligence (AI) is the pre-eminent geopolitical contest of the day. But who is winning the AI race between the United States and China? The answer depends on what you measure. This Data Snapshot compares the inputs and outputs that matter most — from chips and compute to research and innovation — to show which side holds the lead, where the gaps are narrowing, and where capabilities may be overstated.
Based on a thorough analysis of available data, including 14 indicators across four measures — Resources, Technology, AI capabilities, and AI adoption — the United States is currently leading the race. However, its lead is far from uniform, and the competition remains uneven across multiple domains. The United States is well ahead in AI capabilities, driven by its dominance in compute, and in AI adoption, where its lead in web traffic and apps outweighs China’s edge in open models. By contrast, China has a clear lead in Resources, particularly critical minerals — the key materials needed for manufacturing the advanced technologies that make AI possible. Governance, however, remains contested. Neither superpower is widely trusted to regulate AI, leaving room for middle powers such as Australia to help shape the rules.
China holds a clear advantage over the United States in both production and known reserves of critical minerals.
In November 2025, the US Department of the Interior released a list of 60 minerals critical to its economic and national security interests. 1 China leads in production of 30, while the United States is ahead in only eight — with 22 not produced in either country. China holds larger known reserves of 20 listed minerals, and the United States of seven, with one tied, and insufficient data for the remaining 32.
China’s ability to impose targeted export controls on critical minerals poses a major risk for the United States. In 2023, Beijing began announcing restrictions on several, including gallium and germanium — both used in semiconductors. 2
To counter this vulnerability, the United States has sought to cooperate with other countries to secure critical minerals. It has developed Pax Silica, a 24-member international framework focused on AI-related supply chain resilience. 3 In Asia, it has critical minerals frameworks with Australia and Japan and has also signed memoranda of understanding with Malaysia and Thailand. 4 In February 2026, it held a Critical Minerals Ministerial meeting, where it signed an additional 11 bilateral agreements, including one with the Philippines. 5
* For more on the semiconductor supply chain in Asia, and Southeast Asia’s role as a connector between the United States and China, see Between the superpowers: Southeast Asia’s strategic supply chain dilemma (Opens in new window) .
The United States leads China in technological sophistication. While China has almost 11 million full-time equivalent researchers — over seven million more than the United States — US spending on research and development (R&D) is considerably higher as a share of GDP (3.45 per cent versus China’s 2.58 per cent). The United States also has a sizeable lead in the number of data centres and supercomputers.
The United States has sought to limit China’s access to advanced technologies that could help develop its semiconductor industry. Washington has imposed numerous restrictions on both China and Chinese subsidiaries abroad, which has, in turn, spurred affected companies to innovate around them. 6 In May 2026, Huawei announced a new chip-design approach intended to increase transistor density without shrinking transistors. This could allow it to design chips by 2031 with transistor density equivalent to that of the chips Taiwan’s TSMC aims to make in 2028, without the advanced lithography machines China is barred from importing. 7 If successful, this could limit the effect of US export controls.
While companies have looked for ways to work around US controls, Beijing has moved to expand its own, building on its critical mineral restrictions. In October 2026, China proposed adding 40 technologies to its restricted exports, including 23 related to AI — among them AI chip design, the core technology of the most advanced models, and AI tools, such as deepfake detection systems. 8
The United States maintains a lead in AI capabilities. Its AI data centres have nearly 40 times the combined computing power of China’s, and its AI chips 31 times. This has helped US models stay ahead in benchmark tests, though the margin is narrowing.
As of November 2026, the top US large language model (LLM) on Arena, a platform that ranks models through blind head-to-head comparisons, is Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon, with an estimated score of 1528, closely followed by Google’s Gemini 4 Argon at 1520 and Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 at 1509. China’s top model, Moonshot’s Kimi K3, released in mid-July 2026, scores an estimated 1488, placing it 19th. The last top US model at this level was Google’s Gemini 3 Pro, which led from its release in mid-November 2025 until late January 2026. This gap is consistent with claims that the United States has a six-to-nine-month lead in AI capabilities. 9
The global spread of LLMs is arguably the most important front in the AI race. The models that consumers, businesses, and governments rely on will shape the information they see, how their economies run, and, potentially, the future of war. Which country leads depends on how users access the models.
There are six main ways to do so:
Reliable data exist for four of these: websites, apps, self-hosted open models, and aggregator platforms.
China holds a comfortable lead in self-hosted open models and aggregator platforms. 10 In the third quarter of 2026, Chinese models were downloaded nearly 1.8 billion times on Hugging Face, compared with 500 million for US models, giving China 78 per cent of the two countries’ combined downloads. Such models particularly appeal to governments and businesses, which can run them on their own servers to keep data local and adapt them to their needs. On aggregator platform OpenRouter, Chinese models accounted for 55 per cent of all text requests in the week commencing 26 October 2026 — compared to the US share of 38 per cent.
However, most users access LLMs through websites, apps, and embedded AI. The United States has a commanding lead in websites and apps. US models drew more than 90 per cent of combined global traffic to US and Chinese AI websites. US models also accounted for more than 80 per cent of combined use of US and Chinese AI apps, based on Google Play downloads and, for China, where Google Play is unavailable, QuestMobile data.
Overall, most people who use AI rely on US models, giving the United States unmatched reach and greater influence over the technology’s global direction.
With no other country posing a challenge to their dominance in AI, the United States and China have an outsized influence over how the technology is governed globally.
Rival blocs are already taking shape. Washington launched Pax Silica in December 2025 to secure AI supply chains among trusted partners. Beijing answered in July 2026 with the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization (WAICO), which centres on AI governance standards and digital development. articles.title_orig: New Zealand dairy giant Fonterra speeds up China innovation
articles.title_zh: New Zealand dairy giant Fonterra speeds up China innovation
articles.content_orig:
Fonterra Co-operative Group Ltd is accelerating product development with Chinese customers as the New Zealand dairy giant seeks to capture growing demand for protein-rich foods and dairy products tailored to local tastes.
The company is leveraging its six application centers in China to help bakeries, beverage chains and food manufacturers bring new products to market faster, supported by investments in production capacity in New Zealand, CEO Richard Allen said in an interview during the China International Import Expo in Shanghai.
"We know how fast the China market moves and how quickly trends change," Allen said. "Alongside our customers, we can work with them to create new products with new selling points."
A recent visit to Chengdu, Sichuan province, highlighted how much the market had evolved since he worked in China's foodservice sector many years ago.
Allen said dairy products had become more prominent in bakeries, supermarkets and membership stores, with a growing number of products emphasizing their protein content.
Chinese food and beverage brands are also increasingly highlighting the grass-fed origins of New Zealand dairy ingredients to differentiate their products and strengthen their premium positioning.
However, turning those attributes into sales requires products that deliver both quality and value.
Fonterra works with customers to select ingredients that meet nutritional and taste requirements while keeping costs affordable for consumers and commercially viable for producers, Allen said.
"You've got to have nutrition, but it also has to taste good," he said.
Its six application centers in China bring together chefs, marketing specialists and sales teams to develop products suited to local and regional tastes.
For one bakery customer, Fonterra explored incorporating Sichuan's signature mala, or spicy and numbing, flavors into baked goods. Allen also cited the pairing of Anchor butter with pineapple buns as an example of how dairy ingredients can be incorporated into established local food traditions.
"By being on the ground, close to our customers, to their consumers, it allows us to work every day with our customers on developing new products very quickly," he said.
China is also becoming a source of product innovation for Fonterra's operations elsewhere in Asia.
Dairy-topped tea drinks developed in China, for example, have created opportunities among the company's foodservice customers in Southeast Asia, Allen said.
Meanwhile, the overseas expansion of Chinese restaurant and beverage chains is opening another avenue for growth.
As these brands enter international markets, they increasingly seek consistent supplies of familiar ingredients to maintain product quality and taste across their global operations.
Fonterra is supporting Chinese customers expanding into Southeast Asia, the United States, Europe, Australia and New Zealand, drawing on its international supply network and foodservice expertise.
"Not only can we support our local customers in other markets, but we can support Chinese brands in accessing other markets," Allen said.
The strategy builds on Fonterra's established ingredients and foodservice businesses in China, where the cooperative has operated for nearly five decades.
Allen described China as one of Fonterra's cornerstone markets, with demand for dairy ingredients and nutritional products continuing to create opportunities for long-term growth.
To support that demand, Fonterra is investing NZ$150 million ($87 million) to expand ultra-high-temperature cream production at its Edendale facility in New Zealand.
The additional capacity will serve customers in China and other markets, complementing investments in local application centers and culinary, marketing and sales teams.
The expansion comes as Fonterra reported stronger financial results for the year ended July 2026. The cooperative posted revenue of NZ$27 billion and total group operating profit of NZ$3.4 billion in results released on Sept 24.
Fonterra has also announced an additional NZ$1 billion investment over three years to expand its protein manufacturing network in New Zealand's South Island and improve environmental performance.
In China, Allen sees further opportunities in protein-rich products. During his visits to Chinese supermarkets, he was struck by the growing number of products promoting their protein content.
"For us, being agile and moving fast, and ensuring our customers are agile and moving fast, is about being close to the market and really understanding what's happening," Allen said.

articles.title_orig: Putin Seizes Three More Japan Tobacco Businesses, Bringing Takeover to $3.7 Billion
articles.title_zh: Putin Seizes Three More Japan Tobacco Businesses, Bringing Takeover to $3.7 Billion
articles.content_orig:
Russian leader Vladimir Putin has placed three additional subsidiaries of Japan Tobacco International (JTI) under Russian-appointed management, expanding Moscow’s takeover of the Japanese tobacco giant’s operations to seven companies, with the affected assets valued at up to $3.7 billion.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Moscow Times on November 7, the latest presidential decree transferred control of JTI Russia, Pereslavl-Tabak, and JTI Innovative Products to the Russian company Industrial Assets.
The decision follows a separate decree issued on November 5 that placed four JTI manufacturing and tobacco-related businesses under the same management structure.
Bloomberg reported that the newly affected companies include a holding entity, a cigarette distribution business, and an importer of electronic tobacco products and heated tobacco systems.
The earlier takeover covered Petro, JTI Donskoy Tabak, Kres Neva, and JTI Yelets, which collectively employ approximately 4,000 people. According to The Moscow Times, Russian industry analysts estimate the combined value of the affected assets at 250 billion to 300 billion rubles, or approximately $3.1 billion to $3.7 billion.
Industrial Assets was established in September 2026. Russian corporate records identify Sergei Dremov, a former member of the State Council of Russian-occupied Crimea, as one of its founders. His biography indicates that he served in Russian state security agencies between 2000 and 2016.
JTI has operated in Russia since 1999 and previously controlled up to 40% of the country’s cigarette market, selling brands including Winston, Camel, Sobranie, and LD. JTI has operated in Russia since 1999 and previously controlled up to 40% of the country’s cigarette market, selling brands including Winston, Camel, Sobranie, and LD.
Despite Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the company remained in the country, suspending new investments before deciding in 2023 to continue operations.
The expanded takeover follows Japan’s formal protest over Moscow’s initial decision. On November 6, Tokyo demanded that Russia reverse the measure, while Japan’s Foreign Ministry raised the issue with Russian Ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev.

articles.title_orig: Missile strikes multi-story Aramco building in Riyadh’s financial district, witnesses say
articles.title_zh: Missile strikes multi-story Aramco building in Riyadh’s financial district, witnesses say
articles.content_orig:
A building belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco in the financial district in the capital Riyadh has been damaged in a missile attack.
The strike in King Abdullah Financial District was reported after Saudi Civil Defense issued ‌an early-warning ⁠alert of a potential threat to the city.
Video circulating on social media and verified by CNN shows damage to upper floors of the Aramco building, with windows seen blown out. But Saudi authorities said the impact was minimal.
“An administrative building belonging to Saudi Aramco in Riyadh was subjected to an attempted attack,” on Sunday, according to the official Saudi news agency, citing a source at the Saudi Energy Ministry.
“The incident resulted in falling shrapnel that caused minor damage to the building, with no injuries or fatalities reported,” the agency reported.
However, one witness said they saw ambulances heading to the area.
CNN has reached out to the Information Ministry by email for further details.
The Houthis, who have fired missiles and drones towards multiple targets across Saudi Arabia over the last three months, have not claimed responsibility.
Multiple loud booms were ⁠heard in the Saudi capital ⁠Riyadh early Sunday.
The Saudi led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed two cruise missiles in Riyadh and the southern region. Coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki wrote in a post on X that air defenses also “intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Riyadh.”
The missile attacks on Riyadh came a day after Yemen’s Houthi-run health ministry said Saudi airstrikes had ‌killed ‌at least ​33 ​people near the capital Sanaa, including women and children.
“We will punish the Saudi regime for its crimes against the Yemeni people,” said Mahdi al-Mashat, a senior Houthi official, on Saturday.
Last month, 13 people were killed in one missile strike on Riyadh’s international airport, and several more died in other strikes on the airport.
The Houthis have said they will continue firing missiles and drones against Saudi Arabia so long as the Kingdom carries out airstrikes against the parts of Yemen they control and enforces a blockade against its territory.
Saudi Arabia spent $83 billion on defense last year, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, putting it firmly among the top ten military spenders worldwide. It has acquired US fighter jets as well as Patriot and THAAD air defense systems, and a range of advanced weaponry from France and the United Kingdom.
But the Saudis have a lot to defend: a country roughly one-fifth the size of the US, with threats on three sides - from Iran , Iranian-backed militias in Iraq, and the Houthis.
Iran’s hardliners see a weakened Trump – and want more to end the war
The Saudis are intercepting many of the missiles and drones fired by the Houthis. But some get through. The defense ministry faces difficult choices in distributing the existing systems with so many installations vulnerable to attack.
The Houthis have learned to combine ballistic and cruise missiles with long-range drones to overwhelm Saudi defenses, according to analysts.
In Yemen, the Saudi-backed coalition is trying to prevent the Houthis from advancing further south towards the port of Aden, which is held by the internationally-recognized government.
The Houthis have frequently targeted Aden’s airport with missiles in recent weeks, after taking a stretch of Yemen’s Red Sea coast in September.
Hostilities between the Houthis, who are backed by Iran, and Saudi Arabia reignited in July, shattering a 2022 UN-brokered ceasefire that had largely halted fighting ⁠between the ‌two sides.

articles.title_orig: Israel's president taps opposition candidate, not Netanyahu, to form a government
articles.title_zh: Israel's president taps opposition candidate, not Netanyahu, to form a government
articles.content_orig:
Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar ("Straight") party, waves an Israeli flag onstage last month in Tel Aviv following the release of the first exit poll results in Israel's general election. Ariel Schalit/AP hide caption
Israel's president has tapped Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's main political rival, Gadi Eisenkot, to try to form the next government. It's a setback for Netanyahu, whose party won the most seats but failed to secure a parliamentary majority.
Netanyahu's Likud party won 27 seats in last month's election, six more than Eisenkot's Yashar party. But neither secured enough support to command a majority in Israel's 120-seat parliament.
President Isaac Herzog will formally give Eisenkot the mandate at 5 p.m. local time on Sunday. Herzog made the decision after parties representing most of the members of Israel's parliament recommended Eisenkot to try forming a governing coalition.
Eisenkot is a former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, serving as the country's top military commander from 2015 to 2019. A veteran of several military campaigns, he later joined Netanyahu's emergency war cabinet following the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks on Israel, but left the following year, accusing Netanyahu of failing to make progress toward ending the Gaza war and securing the release of hostages.
Eisenkot lost his son, Gal, a reservist killed in Gaza, as well as two nephews during the war.
He leads the center-right Yashar party, which he founded on an anti-corruption and government reform platform. He will now have 28 days to put together a coalition government, with a possible 14-day extension.
That gives him up to six weeks to negotiate with rival parties and secure the 61 seats needed for a parliamentary majority.
The coalition building promises to be a tough task and could include strange bedfellows: from ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties to Arab-led parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel — who make up about 20% of Israel and had a record turnout in these elections.
They could now potentially be the kingmakers. But both Eisenkot and Netanyahu ruled out working with them before the elections. Now there's some public pressure on Eisenkot to change his mind, and on Saturday Netanyahu issued a video warning against that.
He said it would be partnering with what he called Hamas supporters and "those who oppose Judaism." Eisenkot responded, calling Netanyahu's video hysterical.
If Eisenkot fails, Herzog can give another lawmaker a chance to form a government. If those efforts also fail, Israel could face another election. Netanyahu would remain caretaker prime minister in the meantime.

articles.title_orig: China's solar push reshapes life on Tibet's high plateau
articles.title_zh: China's solar push reshapes life on Tibet's high plateau
articles.content_orig:
GONGHE, China – Life has become unexpectedly easier and more lucrative for some shepherds on the world’s highest plateau, after China began carpeting the area with solar panels in a drive to diversify its energy mix.
“It has made grazing much easier for us,” said Li Yonglin, 25, one of those allowed to freely graze their sheep in a fenced solar park in Gonghe, a county in the northwestern province of Qinghai.
“In the morning, we simply open the gate to the sheep pen and don’t really need to look after them. They come back on their own in the evening, and we just pen them up.”
Li estimated the new approach had boosted his earnings to between 50,000 yuan and 60,000 yuan ($7,496.14 and $8,995.37) from 10,000 yuan to 20,000 yuan when he followed the old way.
By July this year, state media said, 6,330 households in five townships had benefited from 56 grazing sites in Hainan, a culturally Tibetan area that encompasses Gonghe, but did not disclose how many got grazing access.
Such early signs suggest China’s projects sprawling over hundreds of acres on the vast Qinghai-Tibet plateau are boosting incomes for some, though researchers and others warn they are also eroding traditional ways of life.
One study estimated the region, sometimes called “the roof of the world,“ where nomadic communities have grazed livestock for millennia, holds almost half of China’s solar energy potential, making it a focal point for renewable energy efforts.
Solar overtook coal in July as the country’s biggest source of installed power capacity, and authorities plan to expand wind and solar power generation by a further 53% in the next five years.
The complex Li visits, sprawling over 148,000 acres (60,000 hectares), uses grazing sheep to reduce mowing costs, said Cao Jun, a safety supervisor for a State Power Investment Corporation project in Hainan.
It leads to a “win-win situation,“ he said, with power generated by the plant sent nationwide to cities such as Beijing, the capital and the commercial hub of Shanghai.
But the integration of livestock and solar infrastructure has not been universally welcomed.
Researchers say solar projects are transforming life on the plateau, where thousands of Tibetan nomads were resettled into rural townships in the early 2000s as the government sought to reverse ecological degradation.
“You can find some places (to graze) around the solar panels, but these are not suitable for nomads and shepherds to hold their livelihood,” said researcher Tsewang Dorji at the Tibet Policy Institute, a think tank of the Tibetan government-in-exile, in India’s hill town of Dharamsala.
Plateau dwellers get little say in the conversion of pastures to solar power projects, said one researcher studying environmental conservation and new energy infrastructure there.
Such installations fragment once-open grazing lands, making herders’ task of watching over livestock harder, added the researcher, who sought anonymity in order to protect collaborators.
Sheep from 16 households were allowed to graze in a solar park for part of the year, the government in Gonghe said in 2024.
A small number of nomads were “tokenistically employed to graze sheep” but goats and yaks were generally excluded, said Mandie McKeown, advocacy director at the environmental charity Foundation for Gaia, which is based in Britain.
Evidence shows “This isn’t pastoralism as it’s traditionally been practiced,” McKeown said.
Wind rattling through solar farm posts and wires produced “persistent and unsettling” sounds that disturbed both people and animals, anthropology researcher Sanggay Tashi at the University of Colorado Boulder said in an article in June, citing people in Qinghai.
Online government records in 2017 showed one undated complaint that Gonghe’s photovoltaic power stations had damaged grasslands, leaving sheep and cattle little grass to eat.
The records, which cited Hainan as the administrative region for the case without identifying the aggrieved person, said an investigation found no truth in the accusation, while adding that grazing was not permitted in the area.
Authorities in Qinghai did not respond to requests for comment.
Not everyone in Gonghe is complaining, though.
“Life has changed tremendously,” said another shepherd, Wen Yujun, who now finds himself able to manage a herd of 700 to 800 largely on his own.
“I never could have imagined it before,” added the 43-year-old, who estimated his annual income had risen eightfold to about 80,000 yuan.

articles.title_orig: Crypto industry braces for reckoning over Trump ties
articles.title_zh: Crypto industry braces for reckoning over Trump ties
articles.content_orig:
This article was contributed by Binance
The second Trump term has put cryptocurrencies on center stage, not only as a policy priority but as a source of real income for the president himself.
The country is suddenly talking about Bitcoin reserves, government-backed stockpiles and Trump’s crypto businesses generating more revenue than his real estate empire. The market is responding in ways not seen before. As of September 25, 2026, the Bitcoin to USD rate was $83,376.06, according to data from Binance. And Washington might have as much influence over the price as basic supply and demand.
In March 2025, Trump signed an executive order creating a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve. This pool was initially filled with Bitcoin already in government hands, seized during various criminal and civil forfeiture cases, according to an official statement from the White House. Alongside that, there’s a Digital Asset Stockpile for other coins. The plan is simple enough: Hold Bitcoin like the U.S. holds gold or oil, and make it a national reserve asset.
More than a year later, this reserve is still mostly for show. The administration keeps insisting that Congress needs to step in before things take off, and while a bill is expected to be reintroduced under a fresh name, so far it’s all been talk, according to Yahoo Finance. Early numbers suggested the government had about 200,000 BTC, though the U.S. Marshals Service isn’t so sure about that, according to CCN.
That Bitcoin reserve was just the warm-up. In July 2025, Trump greenlit the GENIUS Act, the first real federal framework for stablecoins backed by U.S. dollars. Now, payment stablecoins get official recognition: They’re neither securities nor commodities, finally cutting through years of confusion, according to a fact sheet from the White House.
Banks, asset managers and large corporations have shown renewed interest in stablecoins following the regulatory clarity. Regulated stablecoins are becoming a preferred tool for settling tokenized securities and on-chain payments, a shift that could open the door to significant new capital, according to Yahoo Finance and Investing.com. The Trump administration has also appointed crypto-friendly regulators across federal agencies. In May 2026, Trump signed another executive order requiring regulators to drop rules that kept banks from partnering with fintech and crypto companies, according to a fact sheet from the White House .
All these regulatory resets have supercharged the industry and Trump’s business interests. His 2025 financial disclosure, sent to the Office of Government Ethics and made public on June 30, 2026, shows digital assets as his top income stream. His companies pulled in nearly $800 million from World Liberty Financial, the crypto project he co-founded with his sons. That includes $520 million from token sales, and another $250 million by selling stakes in the venture. On top of that, Trump scored another $635 million through sales of the $TRUMP meme coin, which he launched just before returning to office. All this has been reported by Time and Reuters.
Sum it up, and Trump’s family crypto businesses brought in more than $1.4 billion in reported income for 2025. Reuters says crypto was the single biggest driver of his $2.2 billion in total disclosed earnings, beating out real estate and legal settlements combined. When he was called out for it, Trump told reporters, “You know why I’m profiting, because the stock market’s going up, everybody’s profiting,” according to Reuters. For context, his crypto income from the same venture in 2024 was about $57 million, so it grew more than tenfold in just one year, riding the wave of policy changes, according to BBC.
It’s not just empty promises. Companies in the sector have started making real moves thanks to regulatory clarity. Stablecoin issuers, payment platforms and crypto on/off ramp providers are citing the GENIUS Act as the reason they’re ramping up U.S. operations instead of dodging them, according to The Economic Times.
Banks that used to steer clear of crypto because of a 2022 FDIC directive can now roll out digital asset products that follow the rules, according to Legal500.
Dollar moves matter to Bitcoin buyers. The Press Banner’s money column on protecting your portfolio from a falling dollar covers the same concern that has drawn some investors toward Bitcoin during Trump’s second term.
Has the U.S. government bought more Bitcoin for its reserve?
No, not yet. The Strategic Bitcoin Reserve, created in March 2025, only includes Bitcoin seized through criminal and civil cases.
Does the GENIUS Act regulate Bitcoin itself?
No. The GENIUS Act is purely about U.S. dollar-backed stablecoins. It forces issuers to back their tokens one-to-one with cash and Treasury securities, and to publish monthly reserve reports.
How much has Bitcoin moved in September 2026 alone?
It ran from about $76,800 on September 2 to $83,376.06 on September 25, 2026, according to Binance.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine war briefing: Russia ramping up attacks to ‘pressure’ Kyiv at trilateral talks, Zelenskyy says
articles.title_zh: Ukraine war briefing: Russia ramping up attacks to ‘pressure’ Kyiv at trilateral talks, Zelenskyy says
articles.content_orig:
President urges US for support, saying ‘Ukraine must not be left to face this alone’ as barrage plunges cities into darkness. What we know on day 1,719
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of intensifying strikes across the country to put pressure on Kyiv at upcoming talks after an overnight barrage triggered power cuts as temperatures drop. “By intensifying its attacks on Ukraine and our infrastructure at this very moment, Russia is trying to additionally lay the groundwork for putting pressure on Ukraine’s position and that of its partners,” the Ukrainian president said. “Russia perceives diplomacy in its own peculiar way – as a form of aggression.”
Ukraine’s energy ministry said “a massive attack on a number of energy facilities” on Saturday had plunged five regions into darkness and significantly hampered electricity transmission in Kyiv and surrounding regions. Russia had throughout the night launched 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles, Zelenskyy said, among which were KN-23 missiles manufactured and supplied by North Korea.
The strikes came before a US-brokered trilateral meeting in Abu Dhabi scheduled for next week aimed at reviving stalled diplomatic efforts towards peace. Ukrainian officials are expected to sit down with Russian negotiators and US envoys on Tuesday and Wednesday for the first such talks in months. The diplomatic track has been stalled since February when Washington shifted attention to its war with Iran.
Zelenskyy also urged the US to increase its flagging aid to Ukraine. “Unfortunately, there is still a significant shortage of interceptors for Patriot systems, and the United States is in the best position to help address it,” he said.
Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani , on Saturday said he had been targeted by pro-Russian hackers over his backing for Ukraine . Tajani said in a post on X that “backing in a transparent way the freedom and independence of a sovereign state” had made him a target. Tajani said his personal data had been published on the dark web and that the hackers were seeking further information about him and his family and were ‌willing to pay for it.
The Italian prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, who has been one of the strongest backers of Ukraine among western leaders, expressed her support for Tajani and said the sale of confidential information relating to public officials was “a matter of serious concern”. Moscow has not commented ‌on the incident. ‌
France’s far-left presidential contender Jean-Luc Mélenchon said on Saturday that settling the Ukraine conflict could not be done by granting territorial concessions without consulting the people concerned . Melenchon, who polls suggest could reach the second round of next year’s presidential election, set out his France Unbowed party’s foreign policy positions at a rally just outside Paris.
Mélenchon has been criticised in the past for questioning the legitimacy of Zelenskyy. But in a campaign speech to thousands of supporters, he said an administration run by his party would take an active role in settling the war in Ukraine . Europe would have to play an active role in peace talks, he said. “We cannot accept that one could consider a peace with territorial concessions in Ukraine without asking the populations concerned if they agree or not to be on one side or other of the border,” he said. “It is for the people themselves to decide what they want,” he added.
A Ukrainian attack killed one person in Russia’s Belgorod region when a drone hit a private home in the town of Grayvoron, local officials said on Saturday. Russia’s defence ministry said its forces shot down 411 Ukrainian drones overnight over 10 Russian regions, including Belgorod. Drones were also destroyed over the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black and Azov seas, it said. Russian media outlets later reported that the Saratov Oil Refinery had been hit and shared images of plumes of smoke over the city.

articles.content_orig:
Beijing is offering funds and training to help nations win Unesco listings, a move analysts say boosts its soft power
Africa is home to ancient cities, rock art and striking natural landscapes, yet its sites are sorely under-represented on Unesco’s World Heritage List.
According to data released by the UN body, of the 1,273 sites on the list – which are formally protected under the World Heritage Convention treaty – just 115 are in Africa.

articles.title_orig: Ten Months of War to Gain 46 Square Miles: How Russia Is Failing on the Battlefield
articles.title_zh: Ten Months of War to Gain 46 Square Miles: How Russia Is Failing on the Battlefield
articles.content_orig:
Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment
Russian forces continued their missile and drone strike campaign against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure and targeted Kyiv City with 36 ballistic missiles overnight on November 6 to 7. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that Russian forces conducted a massive missile and drone strike campaign against Ukraine overnight, primarily targeting Kyiv City and Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.[1] Zelensky specified that Russian forces targeted 13 oblasts in total, launched 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles, and that all missiles targeted Kyiv City and Kyiv Oblast. Zelensky stated that Russian strikes damaged an electricity substation in Kyiv Oblast connecting the Rivne and Khmelnytskyi nuclear power plants with Kyiv City and Ukraine’s central oblasts and struck substations in Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr, Rivne, Kharkiv, and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts. The Russian Ministry of Defense (MoD) claimed on November 7 that Russian forces struck the Trypilska Thermal Power Plant and the Kyivska and Northern electrical substations in Kyiv Oblast as well as an electrical substation in Zhytomyr Oblast.[2] Russia‘s deliberate targeting of Ukraine’s energy infrastructure corroborates an unconfirmed, intercepted Russian plan that Russian forces would systematically attempt to strike Ukrainian electricity generation and transmission facilities to disconnect Ukraine’s nuclear power plants from a unified grid and cut off Kyiv City from external power supplies.[3] Russia has been increasingly incorporating turbojet engines and mesh radio modems into its long-range strike drones, which is likely allowing Russian forces to more effectively penetrate Ukrainian air defenses and conduct more precise strikes compared to Russia’s Winter 2025-2026 strike campaign. The depletion of Ukraine’s missile interceptors and limited counter-launch capabilities risk leaving Ukraine vulnerable to Russian ballistic missile strikes.
The large-scale Russian ballistic missile strike against Kyiv City also damaged the Northern Bridge, as Russian forces continue efforts to target Ukraine’s transportation infrastructure and disrupt its economy. Kyiv City Mayor Vitaliy Klitschko reported on November 7 that Russian forces damaged the roadbed, trolleybus overhead line, and power line at the Northern Bridge across the Dnipro River in the city.[4] Zelensky stated that Russian forces launched six ballistic missiles at the bridge, four of which struck it.[5] Geolocated footage published on November 7 shows extensive damage to the bridge.[6] Russian forces have repeatedly struck Kyiv City’s Northern and Southern bridges throughout October 2026.[7] Such strikes aim to disrupt the wider Ukrainian economy, sow panic among the population, and significantly degrade civilian life and movement in Ukraine‘s capital.
Ukrainian forces are targeting missile launch sites and ballistic missile production facilities in Russia to reduce Russia’s ability to conduct devastating ballistic missile strikes amidst Ukraine’s dwindling air defense stockpiles. Ukrainian forces struck two Iskander missile launchers and a Pantsir-S1 air defense system in Bryansk Oblast on November 6 and overnight from November 6 to 7, according to the Ukrainian General Staff.[8] The General Staff also reported that Ukrainian forces launched a Neptune cruise missile strike against the Proton-Electrotex Plant in Oryol City, Oryol Oblast (roughly 160 kilometers from the international border), overnight.[9] The Proton-Electrotex Plant produces optoelectronic equipment, including parts for Iskander-M ballistic missiles. Ukraine’s ability to conduct long-range strikes against military assets in Russia is critical for Ukrainian defense against Russian missile strikes ahead of the likely difficult Winter 2026-2027, particularly as Russia’s missile production rate remains high. Ukraine’s Main Military Intelligence Directorate (GUR) reported that Russian forces have stockpiled up to 700 ballistic missiles as of October 2026 and that Russia’s Iskander-M ballistic missile stockpile increased by 13 percent in October compared to August 2026.[10] The GUR added that Russia produces 65 Iskander-M missiles per month.
Western support, including the provision of air defense systems and interceptors, long-range missiles, and reliable low-latency satellite access over Russia, remains vital to Ukraine’s ability to significantly degrade Russia’s drone and missile strike capabilities. The provision of US Tomahawk missiles, for example, would allow Ukraine to strike important military infrastructure that Russia protects in its rear, as ISW has long assessed.[11] Zelensky similarly called on November 5 for Germany to provide Ukraine with Taurus cruise missiles to support the Ukrainian strike campaign against Russian ballistic missile launchers.[12] Even a relatively small number of Western-provided missiles could allow Ukraine to begin systematically targeting Russia’s drone production facilities at the Alabuga Special Economic Zone (SEZ) in the Republic of Tatarstan or the Engels-2 Air Base in Saratov Oblast that houses strategic bombers, which Russian forces use to launch cruise missiles against Ukraine. Ukraine has been using its long-range drones and domestically produced cruise missiles to strike targets deep in the Russian rear, and further Western support would allow Ukraine to degrade Russia’s long-range strike capabilities.
Ukrainian and Russian officials provided further details about the composition of the delegations for the upcoming trilateral negotiations scheduled for November 10 to 11 in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates (UAE). Ukrainian Servant of the People Party Head Davyd Arakhamia stated on November 6 that Foreign Intelligence Service Head Rustem Umerov will lead the Ukrainian delegation, which will also include Presidential Communications Adviser Dmytro Lytvyn, Presidential Office Head Kyrylo Budanov, and Presidential Office First Deputy Head Serhiy Kyslytsya.[13] Russian President Vladimir Putin met with the Russian delegation on November 6, which will include Presidential Aide Vladimir Medinsky, General Staff’s Main Directorate (GRU) Head Admiral Igor Kostyukov, Presidential Aide Yuriy Ushakov, and Deputy Foreign Ministers Mikhail Galuzin and Sergei Ryabkov.[14] Kostyukov led the Russian delegation at the first two rounds of trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi in late January and early February 2026 before Medinsky replaced him to lead the Russian delegation at trilateral negotiations in Geneva, Switzerland, in February 2026. Medinsky notably used his position to stall negotiations by discussing the so-called “historical roots” of the war, the Kremlin’s shorthand for its original maximalist demands.[15] Ushakov is a senior Kremlin official who regularly comments on the status of negotiations with Ukraine and has repeatedly reiterated the Kremlin’s maximalist demands that Ukraine make unilateral concessions before Russia agrees to engage in any meaningful peace negotiations.[16] Galuzin was a member of the Russian delegation to negotiations in Istanbul, Turkey, as well as Geneva in May 2025 and February 2026, respectively, and has reiterated the need to address the so-called “root causes” of the war.[17] Ryabkov has not formally participated in peace negotiations but frequently claims that Russia can only accept peace proposals that align with Putin’s war aims and “ground realities.” Ryabkov routinely reiterates Russia’s commitment to the alleged US-Russia agreements following the Alaska Summit in August 2025, despite the lack of public statements following the summit and no confirmation that any agreement was reached.[18] Ryabkov also facilitated the Kremlin’s 2021 ultimatums to the United States and NATO member states, which amounted to the destruction of the current NATO alliance under the guise of “security guarantees” for Russia.[19] The Kremlin appears to be sending a delegation of officials who previously stalled neg
